topics.title: Revision sheet: skeleton and muscles
topics.source: Class revision sheet (Q1 and Q2, 12 marks). Questions as printed; diagrams redrawn. The sheet prints no answers — these are ours.
topics.summary: The two questions from the class revision sheet: the skeleton and joints (Q1), and muscles, tendons and antagonistic pairs in the arm and leg (Q2).

images.caption: Q1: the human skeleton, with the labels from the sheet. In (a) you draw a line from J to one joint in the leg.
Q1 (d): part of the arm. Part A is the biceps, part B the triceps.
Q2: muscles and bones of a human arm.

Q2 (c): muscles and bones of a human leg (toes on the left). D = quadriceps (front of thigh), A = hamstrings (back of thigh), C = tibialis anterior (front of shin), B = gastrocnemius (calf, with the soleus underneath).

facts: Q1 (a): joints in the leg — **hip**, **knee** and **ankle**. We need joints so the skeleton can **bend and move**.
Q1 (b): the **ribs** move so we can breathe; the **lower jaw** moves so we can chew food.
Q1 (c): **calcium** is needed in the diet for strong bones and teeth.
Q1 (d): parts A and B are **muscles**. When part A (the biceps) gets shorter, the lower arm moves **up**.
Q2 (a): tendons must **not stretch**, so that when the muscle contracts its pull moves the bone (none of the pull is lost).
Q2 (b): **antagonistic pair** — the two muscles work against each other: when one **contracts**, the other **relaxes**.

Q2 (c): **C** (the **tibialis anterior**, front of the shin) contracts to lift the toes, while **B** (the **gastrocnemius**, calf) relaxes. The antagonistic pairs are **B and C** and **D and A** (**quadriceps** and **hamstrings**).
keywords: where two bones meet so the skeleton can move
pulls on a bone when it contracts
joins muscle to bone; does not stretch
one contracts while the other relaxes

questions.stem: Q1 (a)(i) On the sheet you draw a line from the letter J to one joint in the leg. Name one joint in the leg.
questions.explain: The leg has three main joints: hip, knee and ankle.

questions.stem: Q1 (a)(ii) Why do we need joints in our skeleton?
questions.answer: so that the skeleton can bend and we can move
choices: so that the bones can make blood cells
so that the organs are protected
so that the bones are stronger
questions.explain: Joints are where bones meet; they let the skeleton bend so we can move.

questions.stem: Q1 (b)(i) Which part of our skeleton, labelled in the diagram, moves so that we can breathe?
questions.explain: The ribs move up and out when we breathe in, and down and in when we breathe out.

questions.stem: Q1 (b)(ii) Which part of our skeleton, labelled in the diagram, moves so that we can chew food?
questions.explain: Only the lower jaw moves — the upper jaw is fixed to the skull.

questions.stem: Q1 (c) Which one of the following is needed in the diet for strong bones and teeth?
questions.explain: Calcium (from milk, cheese, yoghurt, green vegetables) builds strong bones and teeth.

questions.stem: Q1 (d)(i) Parts A and B are attached to bones. What name is given to parts of the body like parts A and B?
questions.explain: A and B are muscles (biceps and triceps), attached to the bones by tendons.

questions.stem: Q1 (d)(ii) Part A gets shorter. In which direction does the lower arm move?
questions.explain: Part A (the biceps) contracts and pulls the lower arm up — the arm bends at the elbow.

questions.stem: Q2 (a) Why is it important that the tendons do not stretch?
questions.answer: so that when the muscle contracts, its pull moves the bone
choices: so that the muscle can get longer
so that the bones can bend
so that the joint does not need cartilage
questions.explain: If tendons stretched, some of the muscle's pull would be lost and the bone would not move properly.

questions.stem: Q2 (b) The biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair of muscles. What does this mean?
questions.answer: they work against each other: when one contracts, the other relaxes
choices: they both contract at the same time
one pushes the bone and the other pulls it
questions.explain: Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: biceps contracts to bend the arm, triceps contracts to straighten it.

questions.stem: Q2 (c)(i) Which muscle contracts to move the foot in the direction shown by the arrow? Give the letter.
questions.explain: C is the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin: it contracts to lift the toes, while B (the gastrocnemius, calf) relaxes.

questions.stem: Q2 (c)(ii) Which two pairs of muscles are antagonistic pairs? (The sheet asks you to tick two boxes.)
questions.answer: B and C, and D and A
choices: A and B, and C and D
A and B, and B and C
C and D, and D and A
questions.explain: Each pair works across one joint: D and A (quadriceps and hamstrings) move the knee; B and C (gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior) move the ankle.

topics.title: Handout: the skeletal system
topics.source: Class handout “The Skeletal System” (Lesson 1). The sheet is blank to fill in — the answers here are ours, so check them against what you wrote in class.
topics.summary: The three parts of the handout: the bones of the skeletal system, the functions of the skeleton (with the benefit to performance), and the types of connective tissue.

images.caption: Bones of the skeletal system — the handout asks you to label them. Hide the names to test yourself.

table.title: Functions of the skeleton
head: Function
Explanation
Benefit to performance
rows: Gives the body its shape and holds it upright; muscles and organs hang on it.
A firm frame for good posture and technique, e.g. a balanced stance in gymnastics.
Bones surround vital organs: the skull protects the brain, the ribs the heart and lungs, the vertebrae the spinal cord.
You can take part in contact sports (a rugby tackle, a header) with less risk of serious injury.
Muscles are attached to bones by tendons and pull on them; bones act as levers at the joints.
Lets you run, jump, throw and kick.
Red and white blood cells are made in the bone marrow.
Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles, so you can keep going for longer; white blood cells fight infection.
Strong bones break less easily; calcium is also needed for muscles to contract.

facts: **Ligaments** join **bone to bone** at a joint. They are strong and slightly stretchy, and hold the joint together so it stays stable.
**Tendons** join **muscle to bone**. They are strong and do **not stretch**, so the pull of the muscle moves the bone.
**Cartilage** covers the **ends of the bones** at a joint. It is smooth and rubbery: it stops the bones rubbing together (less friction) and absorbs shock.
keywords: smooth cushion on the ends of bones
how a function helps you in sport

questions.stem: Which function of the skeleton gives the body its shape and holds it upright?
questions.explain: Support: the skeleton is the frame that holds the body up.

questions.stem: A rugby player is tackled hard but their heart and lungs are not hurt. Which function of the skeleton helped?
questions.explain: Protection: the ribs protect the heart and lungs.

questions.stem: Muscles pull on bones, which act as levers at the joints. Which function of the skeleton is this?
questions.explain: Movement: muscles pull bones at joints.

questions.stem: How does making red blood cells help a long-distance runner?
questions.answer: they carry oxygen to the working muscles
questions.explain: Red blood cells (made in the bone marrow) carry oxygen to the muscles, so the runner can keep going for longer.

questions.stem: In which part of a bone are blood cells made?
questions.explain: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

questions.stem: Which mineral stored in bones helps them stay strong and helps muscles contract?
questions.explain: Bones store calcium (and phosphorus).

questions.stem: Which type of connective tissue joins bone to bone?
questions.explain: Ligaments join bone to bone and hold a joint together.

questions.stem: Which type of connective tissue joins muscle to bone?
questions.explain: Tendons join muscle to bone.

questions.stem: Which type of connective tissue covers the ends of the bones and stops them rubbing together?
questions.explain: Cartilage is smooth and rubbery: it reduces friction and absorbs shock.

questions.stem: Tendons stretch a lot so that the muscle can move freely.
questions.explain: Tendons do not stretch — so all the pull of the muscle moves the bone.

questions.stem: Ligaments hold the bones of a joint together and keep it stable.
questions.explain: Ligaments join bone to bone and stop the joint moving too far.

questions.stem: Why is cartilage useful in a joint when you land from a jump?
questions.answer: it absorbs shock and stops the bones rubbing
choices: it joins the muscle to the bone
questions.explain: Cartilage cushions the ends of the bones.

topics.title: Fix my test: Part 1 test
topics.source: Your Part 1 test (Foundation), November 2026 — aimed at the marks that got away. The questions are ours, not the test's.
topics.summary: The mix-ups and missing bits from the test, plus the longer “describe” and “explain” answers. Practise until these are automatic.

table.title: The mix-ups
head: Easy to swap
Remember
rows: knee = hinge (bends one way, like a door); shoulder = ball and socket (swings round in a circle)
ligament joins bone to bone; cartilage is the smooth cushion on the ends of bones; tendon joins muscle to bone
ribs protect the heart and lungs; the backbone protects the spinal cord
same bones, different jobs: flying versus lifting, holding and gripping

facts: **Knee = hinge joint**, **shoulder = ball and socket**. Test it: your knee only bends one way; your shoulder can swing your arm right round.

**Ligaments** join **bone to bone**. **Cartilage** is the smooth, rubbery layer on the ends of bones that **reduces friction**. **Tendons** join **muscle to bone**. **Bone marrow** makes **blood cells**.
The **backbone** (vertebral column) protects the **spinal cord**. The **ribs** protect the **heart and lungs**. The **skull** protects the **brain**.
Jobs of the skeleton, in exam words: **support**, **protection**, **movement**, **making blood cells**.

Microscope: cells are **too small to see with the naked eye** → the microscope **magnifies** them. The sample is **thin** so **light passes through**. A **stain** (iodine, methylene blue) makes cells **easier to see**.
Organ systems: **respiratory** = oxygen in, carbon dioxide out; **circulatory** = transports substances; **digestive** = breaks down and absorbs food; **reproductive** = produces sperm and eggs.

**Describe and explain answers:** count the marks — a 2-mark question needs **two** points, a 4-mark question **four** steps, a 6-mark question six points written in order with the key words (contracts, relaxes, pulls, tendon, antagonistic).
keywords: shoulder, hip — moves in all directions
smooth layer on the ends of bones, reduces friction

questions.stem: What type of joint is the knee?
questions.explain: Your knee bends one way only, like a door hinge.

questions.stem: What type of joint is the shoulder?
questions.explain: The top of the humerus is a ball sitting in a cup in the shoulder blade — it swings in all directions.

questions.stem: Which pair are BOTH hinge joints?
questions.explain: Knee and elbow bend one way; shoulder and hip are ball and socket.

questions.stem: Which tissue connects two bones together?
questions.explain: Ligament = bone to bone.

questions.stem: Which tissue reduces friction between bones?
questions.explain: Cartilage is smooth and slippery, so the bone ends don't rub.

questions.stem: Which tissue connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.explain: Tendon = muscle to bone.

questions.stem: Which tissue produces blood cells?
questions.explain: Bone marrow is the soft tissue inside some bones.

questions.stem: Name the part of the body that is protected by the backbone.
questions.explain: The vertebrae surround the spinal cord. Lungs and heart are protected by the ribs.

questions.stem: Which is a job of the skeleton, in the words the exam wants?
questions.explain: Support, protection, movement and making blood cells.

questions.stem: What is added to cells to make them easier to see?
questions.explain: Light is needed too — but the thing ADDED to the cells is a stain.

questions.stem: Why must a sample be very thin when you look at it under a microscope?
questions.answer: so light can pass through it
choices: so it is easier to cut
so it doesn't need a stain
questions.explain: Light comes up from below through the sample — too thick and you'd see nothing.

questions.stem: Which organ system replaces oxygen and removes carbon dioxide from the blood?
questions.explain: Lungs → respiratory (gas exchange) system.

questions.stem: Which organ system produces sperm and eggs?
questions.explain: The reproductive system makes the sex cells.

questions.stem: Which muscle contracts to bend your arm?
questions.explain: Biceps contracts (pulls), triceps relaxes. To straighten, it's the other way round.

questions.stem: Muscles can push as well as pull.
questions.explain: False — muscles can only pull. That's why they work in antagonistic pairs.

questions.stem: Explain why you need a microscope to look at cells.

acceptablePoints.point: cells are too small to see with the naked eye (just your eyes)
the microscope magnifies them / makes them look bigger, so you can see them or their parts

award.2: one mark for each point, up to 2

markScheme.modelAnswer: Cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so the microscope magnifies them — it makes them look bigger so we can see the cells and their parts.

questions.stem: Describe how to use a microscope to see onion cells on a slide with a ×20 objective lens.

acceptablePoints.point: put the slide on the stage and hold it with the stage clips
start with the lowest-power objective lens
use the coarse focusing wheel to get the cells roughly in focus (bringing the lens close while looking from the side)
use the fine focusing wheel to make the image sharp
turn to the ×20 objective and refocus with the fine wheel

award.4: any four of the points, in a sensible order

markScheme.modelAnswer: Put the slide on the stage and hold it with the clips. Turn to the lowest-power objective. Looking from the side, bring the lens close to the slide with the coarse wheel, then look through the eyepiece and turn the coarse wheel until the cells appear. Sharpen the image with the fine wheel. Then turn to the ×20 objective and refocus with the fine wheel.

questions.stem: The skeleton protects parts of the body. Give two other jobs of the skeleton.

acceptablePoints.point: support (holds the body up / gives it shape)
movement (muscles pull on bones at joints)
making blood cells (in the bone marrow)
storing minerals such as calcium

markScheme.modelAnswer: Support — it holds the body up. Movement — muscles pull on the bones. (Making blood cells in the bone marrow also counts.)

questions.stem: A bird's wing has the same bones as a human arm. Describe the difference in the job (function) of a bird's wing and a human arm.

acceptablePoints.point: the wing is used for flying (flapping to lift the bird / push air)
the arm is used for lifting, carrying, holding or gripping things (with the hand)

award.2: the job of the wing AND the job of the arm
award.1: the job of one of them

markScheme.modelAnswer: A bird uses its wing to fly — flapping pushes air down and lifts it. A human uses their arm and hand to lift, carry and hold things.

questions.tip: Careful: it asks about the JOB, not the type of joint.

questions.stem: Describe in detail how the muscles work to bend the arm and then straighten it again.

acceptablePoints.point: muscles can only pull (contract), they cannot push
to bend the arm the biceps contracts
while the biceps contracts, the triceps relaxes
the muscle pulls on the bone (forearm) through a tendon / the arm bends at the elbow (a hinge joint)
to straighten the arm the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes
the biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair — they work against each other

award.6: one mark for each point, up to 6

markScheme.modelAnswer: Muscles can only pull, not push. To bend the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes; the biceps pulls on the forearm bone through a tendon, so the arm bends at the elbow, a hinge joint. To straighten it, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. Because they pull in opposite directions, the biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair.

questions.tip: Six marks: give six points, in order, with the key words — and check your spelling (biceps, triceps, contracts, antagonistic).

topics.title: Working out speed
topics.summary: What speed means, how to calculate it from distance and time, and average speed for a whole journey.

table.title: Some typical speeds
head: Moving thing
About how fast
rows: a car on a motorway (70 mph)

facts: **Speed** tells you how much distance something covers in a certain amount of time.
**speed = distance ÷ time**. With distance in **metres (m)** and time in **seconds (s)**, speed comes out in **metres per second (m/s)**.
Turn it round when you need to: **distance = speed × time** and **time = distance ÷ speed**.
Example: a runner covers 100 m in 20 s. Speed = 100 ÷ 20 = **5 m/s**.
The **higher the speed**, the **shorter the time** a journey takes.
Real journeys speed up, slow down and stop. **Average speed = total distance ÷ total time** for the whole journey.
Other units of speed: **km/h** (kilometres per hour) and **mph** (miles per hour), used for cars and trains.
Measuring speed: measure the **distance** with a metre rule or tape measure and the **time** with a stopwatch (or light gates, which are more accurate). Repeat and take a **mean**.

Toy car down a slope: the **height of the slope** is what you change (independent variable), the **speed** is what you measure (dependent variable); keep the car and the distance the same (control variables).
keywords: how much distance is covered in a certain time
total distance ÷ total time for a whole journey
the unit of speed when distance is in m and time in s
times an object electronically as it passes through a beam
the thing you change in an experiment
something you keep the same to make it a fair test

questions.stem: Which is the formula for speed?
questions.explain: Speed is distance covered per unit of time, so you divide the distance by the time.

questions.stem: What is the unit of speed when distance is in metres and time is in seconds?
questions.explain: Metres divided by seconds gives metres per second, written m/s.

questions.stem: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is her speed, in m/s?
questions.explain: speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: A car travels 300 m in 15 s. What is its speed, in m/s?
A cyclist rides at 6 m/s for 50 s. How far does he go, in metres?
questions.explain: distance = speed × time = 6 × 50 = 300 m.

questions.stem: A walker moves at 1.5 m/s. How long does it take her to walk 450 m, in seconds?
questions.explain: time = distance ÷ speed = 450 ÷ 1.5 = 300 s (that is 5 minutes).

questions.stem: A bus travels 1200 m in 200 s, including two stops. What is its average speed, in m/s?
questions.explain: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 1200 ÷ 200 = 6 m/s. The stops are part of the total time.

questions.stem: A train travels 90 km in 1.5 hours. What is its average speed, in km/h?
questions.explain: Average speed = 90 ÷ 1.5 = 60 km/h. Kilometres ÷ hours gives km/h.

questions.stem: What is average speed?
questions.answer: the total distance divided by the total time for a journey
choices: the fastest speed reached on a journey
the speed at the very end of a journey
the total time divided by the total distance
questions.explain: Average speed treats the whole journey as if it were at one steady speed: total distance ÷ total time.

questions.stem: Two cars drive the same distance. The faster car takes less time.
questions.explain: A higher speed covers each metre more quickly, so the same journey takes less time.

questions.stem: A speed of 10 m/s means the object travels 10 metres every minute.
questions.explain: m/s means metres per second: 10 m/s is 10 metres every second (600 metres a minute).

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment would you use to time a toy car rolling down a ramp?
questions.explain: A stopwatch measures time. Light gates connected to a timer do it more accurately, because they don't rely on your reaction time.

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment would you use to measure the distance the toy car rolls?
questions.explain: Distance is measured with a metre rule or a tape measure.

questions.stem: In a toy car experiment, you change the height of the slope and measure the car's speed. What is the height of the slope?
questions.explain: The independent variable is the one you choose to change. The speed, which you measure, is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: In the same experiment, which of these should you keep the same to make it a fair test?
questions.answer: the toy car and the distance it rolls
questions.explain: Control variables stay the same, so that only the slope height can be causing a change in speed.

questions.stem: Why should you time the car several times and work out a mean?
questions.answer: to reduce the effect of random errors, such as your reaction time
choices: to make the car go faster each time
so that all the results come out the same
because the stopwatch needs to warm up
questions.explain: Each timing can be a little off (you press the button late or early). Averaging several repeats makes the result more reliable.

topics.title: Distance–time graphs
topics.summary: How to read a journey from a distance–time graph and work out speed from it.

images.caption: One journey on a distance–time graph: what each part of the line means.
A walk with numbers: work out the speed in each section from the graph.

facts: A **distance–time graph** shows a journey: **distance** goes up the side (y-axis), **time** goes along the bottom (x-axis).
A **straight sloping line** means a **steady (constant) speed**.
The **steeper** the line, the **faster** the object is moving.
A **flat (horizontal) line** means the object is **stationary** (stopped): time goes on but the distance doesn't change.
A **curving line** means the speed is changing: getting **steeper** = **accelerating** (speeding up); getting **flatter** = **decelerating** (slowing down).
**Speed from the graph:** pick a straight section, read off the **distance travelled** and the **time taken**, then divide: speed = distance ÷ time.
**Acceleration** is how quickly the speed increases or decreases.
keywords: a graph showing how far something has gone at each time
how steep a line is — on this graph it shows the speed
the same speed all the time (straight sloping line)
how quickly speed increases or decreases

questions.stem: On the graph, what is the object doing in the part labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The line curves and gets steeper: the object covers more distance every second, so it is speeding up.

questions.stem: On the graph, what is the object doing in the part labelled {L}?
questions.explain: A straight, steep line: the same (large) distance every second, so a fast steady speed.

questions.stem: On the graph, what is the object doing in the part labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The line curves and gets flatter: less distance every second, so it is slowing down.

questions.stem: On the graph, what is the object doing in the part labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The line is flat: time passes but the distance stays the same, so the object is not moving.

questions.stem: On the graph, what is the object doing in the part labelled {L}?
questions.explain: A straight line that is not very steep: a small, equal distance every second, so a slow steady speed.

questions.stem: Use the graph. What is the walker's speed in section A, in m/s?
questions.explain: In section A the walker goes 200 m in 40 s: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: Use the graph. What is the walker's speed in section B, in m/s?
questions.explain: The line is flat from 40 s to 60 s: the distance stays at 200 m, so the walker has stopped.

questions.stem: Use the graph. What is the walker's speed in section C, in m/s?
questions.explain: From 60 s to 100 s the distance goes from 200 m to 300 m: 100 m in 40 s, so 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5 m/s.

questions.stem: Use the graph. What is the walker's average speed for the whole 100 s, in m/s?
questions.explain: Total distance 300 m ÷ total time 100 s = 3 m/s. The stop counts as part of the time.

questions.stem: Use the graph. In which section is the walker moving fastest?
questions.explain: Section A has the steepest line, so the walker covers distance fastest there.

questions.stem: On a distance–time graph, what does a steeper straight line show?
questions.explain: Steeper means more distance in the same time — a higher speed. Straight means the speed is steady.

questions.stem: What does a flat (horizontal) line on a distance–time graph show?
choices: the object is moving at a steady speed
the object is going back to the start
questions.explain: Flat means the distance is not changing while time goes on, so the object is not moving.

questions.stem: A line on a distance–time graph curves and gets steeper and steeper. What is the object doing?
questions.explain: Getting steeper means the object covers more distance every second, so its speed is increasing.

questions.stem: A straight sloping line on a distance–time graph shows a constant speed.
questions.explain: A straight line means the same distance is covered every second, so the speed doesn't change.

questions.stem: A curved line on a distance–time graph means the object has stopped.
questions.explain: A curved line means the speed is changing (speeding up or slowing down). A stopped object gives a flat line.

questions.stem: What is the word for how quickly an object's speed increases or decreases?
questions.explain: Acceleration describes how quickly speed changes. Slowing down is sometimes called deceleration.

questions.stem: On a distance–time graph, which axis is time plotted on?
questions.explain: Time goes along the bottom (the x-axis); distance goes up the side (the y-axis).

questions.stem: A cyclist rides to school. She rides at a steady speed, stops at some traffic lights, then rides on more slowly at a steady speed. Describe the shape of the distance–time graph for her trip.

acceptablePoints.point: a straight sloping line for the first, steady part of the ride
a flat / horizontal line while she waits at the lights (distance not changing)
then a straight line that is less steep (shallower) than the first, because she is slower
the line never slopes downwards — her distance from home keeps going up or stays the same

markScheme.modelAnswer: First a straight sloping line, because she rides at a steady speed. At the lights the line goes flat, because her distance doesn't change while time passes. Then another straight sloping line, but less steep than the first, because she is now going more slowly.

questions.tip: Say what each part of the line looks like and why.

topics.title: Forces, motion and relative speed
topics.summary: How the overall force on an object changes its motion, and why speed depends on who is watching.

images.caption: Two cars on a road: their speeds look different to each driver and to the person by the road.

facts: The **resultant force** is the single overall force on an object: **add** forces that act in the same direction, **subtract** forces that act in opposite directions.
If the resultant force is **zero** (forces **balanced**), the motion **does not change**: a still object stays still, and a moving object keeps the same speed and direction.
If the resultant force is **not zero** (forces **unbalanced**), the motion **changes**: the object **speeds up, slows down or changes direction**.
Forward force **bigger** than the backward forces → **speeds up**. Backward forces (friction, air resistance) **bigger** → **slows down**.
**Relative motion:** the speed you measure depends on how **you** are moving. Speeds are always measured **relative to an observer**.
Two objects going the **same way**: each sees the other moving at the **difference** of their speeds (30 m/s and 25 m/s → 5 m/s).
Two objects going in **opposite directions**: each sees the other moving at the **sum** of their speeds (20 m/s and 15 m/s → 35 m/s).
A passenger sitting on a train sees the person opposite as **not moving**; someone on the platform sees them both moving at the **train's speed**.
keywords: the overall force when all the forces are added up
forces that cancel out — the resultant is zero
forces that don't cancel — the motion changes
different observers judge a speed differently if they are moving too
a force from the air that pushes against a moving object
a force between surfaces that acts against movement

questions.stem: A car's engine pushes it forward with 500 N. Friction and air resistance push back with 500 N. What is the resultant force, in N?
questions.explain: The forces are equal and opposite: 500 − 500 = 0 N. They are balanced.

questions.stem: The car in the last question is already moving. With balanced forces it keeps going at the same speed.
questions.explain: Balanced forces don't stop a moving object — its motion just doesn't change, so it keeps the same speed and direction.

questions.stem: A boat's engine pushes forward with 800 N and the water pushes back with 300 N. What is the resultant force, in N?
questions.explain: The forces act in opposite directions, so subtract: 800 − 300 = 500 N forwards.

questions.stem: The boat's engine pushes with 800 N and the water pushes back with 300 N. What happens to the boat?
questions.explain: There is a resultant force of 500 N forwards, so the boat accelerates.

questions.stem: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road. Why does she slow down?
questions.answer: friction and air resistance are now bigger than any forward force
choices: the forces on her are balanced
questions.explain: With no forward push, the backward forces win: the resultant force is backwards, so she slows down.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a change in motion?
questions.answer: moving at a steady speed in a straight line
choices: turning a corner at the same speed
questions.explain: A change of speed or a change of direction is a change in motion. Steady speed in a straight line is no change.

questions.stem: A ball going round in a circle at a steady speed has a resultant force on it.
questions.explain: Its direction keeps changing, and a change of direction needs an unbalanced (resultant) force.

questions.stem: If the forces on a moving object are balanced, it will slowly come to a stop.
questions.explain: Balanced forces mean no change in motion — it keeps moving at the same speed. Things slow down only when there is a backward resultant force.

questions.stem: A skydiver opens her parachute. Air resistance is now much bigger than her weight. What happens?
choices: she stops in mid-air straight away
questions.explain: The resultant force is upwards while she is still falling, so she keeps falling but more and more slowly.

questions.stem: Car P drives at 30 m/s and car Q at 25 m/s, the same way. How fast does car P seem to move to the driver of car Q, in m/s?
questions.explain: Same direction, so take the difference: 30 − 25 = 5 m/s. Car P slowly pulls ahead.

questions.stem: How fast is car P moving for the person standing still by the road, in m/s?
questions.explain: The person by the road isn't moving, so they see car P's full speed: 30 m/s.

questions.stem: How does car Q look to the driver of car P?
questions.answer: it seems to drift backwards at 5 m/s
choices: it seems to move forwards at 25 m/s
it seems to move forwards at 55 m/s
questions.explain: Car P is 5 m/s faster, so from P car Q falls further and further behind, as if it were moving backwards at 5 m/s.

questions.stem: Two cars drive towards each other, one at 20 m/s and the other at 15 m/s. How fast does each driver see the other car coming, in m/s?
questions.explain: Opposite directions, so add the speeds: 20 + 15 = 35 m/s.

questions.stem: You sit on a train moving at 40 m/s. How fast does the passenger sitting opposite you seem to move?
questions.answer: 0 m/s — they seem to stay still
questions.explain: You are both moving together at the same speed, so relative to you they are not moving at all.

questions.stem: What is the name for the idea that a speed you measure depends on how you, the observer, are moving?
questions.explain: Relative motion: different observers judge a speed differently if they are moving too.

questions.stem: What is the name for the single overall force on an object when all the forces are added up?
questions.explain: The resultant force is what decides whether the motion changes.

questions.stem: Runner X runs at 6 m/s and runner Y runs at 4 m/s, in the same direction along a straight track. A coach stands still beside the track. Describe how fast each runner seems to move to the coach, and how the runners seem to move to each other.

acceptablePoints.point: the coach (not moving) sees X at 6 m/s and Y at 4 m/s
the runners see each other moving at the difference of their speeds: 2 m/s
to X, runner Y seems to fall behind / move backwards
to Y, runner X seems to pull ahead / move away forwards
the speed you see depends on how you are moving yourself (relative motion)

award.4: any four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: The coach is standing still, so he sees the real speeds: X at 6 m/s and Y at 4 m/s. The runners are both moving the same way, so to each other the speed is the difference, 6 − 4 = 2 m/s. To X, runner Y seems to slip backwards at 2 m/s; to Y, runner X seems to pull ahead at 2 m/s. This is relative motion: the speed you see depends on how you are moving.

questions.tip: Give numbers, and say what each runner sees.

topics.title: Mass and weight
topics.summary: Mass is the amount of stuff in an object; weight is the pull of gravity on it, worked out with W = m × g.

images.caption: The same astronaut on Earth and on the Moon: same mass, different weight (arrows drawn to scale).

table.title: Mass or weight?
head: Mass
Weight
rows: the amount of stuff (matter) in an object
the force of gravity pulling on an object

facts: **Mass** is the amount of **stuff (matter)** in an object, measured in **kilograms (kg)**. It is the same wherever the object is.
**Weight** is a **force**: the pull of **gravity** on an object, measured in **newtons (N)**.
**weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)** — W = m × g.
**Gravitational field strength (g)** is the force of gravity on each kilogram. **On Earth g = 10 N/kg; on the Moon g = 1.6 N/kg.**
Example: a 50 kg pupil weighs 50 × 10 = **500 N** on Earth, but only 50 × 1.6 = **80 N** on the Moon. Their mass is 50 kg in both places.
Weight depends on **two** things: the object's **mass** and the **strength of gravity** where it is.
In everyday talk people say "I weigh 45 kg" — scientifically that is your **mass**. Your weight is about 450 N.
Weight is measured with a **newtonmeter** (a spring that stretches); mass with a **balance**.

On a trip to the Moon an astronaut's **mass stays the same**, but her **weight falls** as she leaves Earth (Earth's pull gets weaker), is **almost zero** far out in space, then rises to about **one sixth** of her Earth weight on the Moon.
keywords: the amount of stuff in an object (kg)
the force of gravity on an object (N)
the unit of force, including weight
the force of gravity on 1 kg (N/kg)

questions.stem: What is the unit of weight?
questions.explain: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons (N).

questions.stem: What is the unit of mass?
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of stuff, measured in kilograms (kg).

questions.stem: Which is the formula for weight?
questions.explain: W = m × g: weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg).

questions.stem: What is the gravitational field strength (g) on Earth, in N/kg?
questions.explain: On Earth g is about 10 N/kg (more exactly 9.8 N/kg): every kilogram is pulled down with about 10 N.

questions.stem: What is the gravitational field strength (g) on the Moon, in N/kg?
questions.explain: On the Moon g = 1.6 N/kg, about one sixth of Earth's, because the Moon has much less mass.

What would the same 50 kg pupil weigh on the Moon, in N? (g = 1.6 N/kg)
questions.explain: W = m × g = 50 × 1.6 = 80 N. Her mass is still 50 kg.

questions.stem: A bag of sugar has a mass of 2 kg. What does it weigh on Earth, in N?
A rock weighs 30 N on Earth. What is its mass, in kg?
questions.explain: mass = weight ÷ g = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 kg.

questions.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon, in kg?
questions.explain: Mass doesn't change from place to place — she is made of the same amount of stuff. Only her weight changes.

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment measures weight?
questions.explain: A newtonmeter measures forces, including weight. A balance measures mass.

questions.stem: What happens to your mass if you travel to the Moon?
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of stuff in you, which doesn't depend on where you are. Your weight is what changes.

questions.stem: Mass is a force.
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of stuff in an object (kg). Weight is the force (N).

questions.stem: You weigh less on the Moon because the Moon's gravitational field strength is smaller than Earth's.
questions.explain: W = m × g: your mass is the same, but g is only 1.6 N/kg on the Moon, so your weight is smaller.

questions.stem: Someone says "I weigh 45 kg." What is the scientific mistake?
questions.answer: kg is a unit of mass — weight is a force, measured in newtons
choices: kg is a unit of length
weight should be measured in N/kg
questions.explain: 45 kg is their mass. Their weight on Earth is 45 × 10 = 450 N.

questions.stem: What is the name for the force of gravity on each kilogram of mass?
questions.explain: Gravitational field strength (g), in N/kg, is the force on every kilogram.

questions.stem: A space probe's weight gets smaller as it flies away from Earth. Why?
questions.answer: Earth's pull gets weaker further away, so g gets smaller
choices: its mass gets smaller as it goes
there is no air in space
questions.explain: Weight = m × g. The mass stays the same, but g falls with distance from Earth.

questions.stem: An astronaut travels from the Earth to the Moon. Describe and explain how her mass and her weight change during the journey.

acceptablePoints.point: her mass stays the same all the way (the amount of stuff in her doesn't change)
weight is the force of gravity on her: weight = mass × gravitational field strength
as she moves away from Earth, Earth's gravity gets weaker (g falls), so her weight gets smaller
far out in space, between Earth and Moon, her weight is very small / almost zero
as she gets closer to the Moon, the Moon's gravity pulls on her more strongly
on the Moon g = 1.6 N/kg instead of 10 N/kg, so her weight is about one sixth of her Earth weight
a correct example calculation, e.g. 60 kg × 10 = 600 N on Earth and 60 kg × 1.6 = 96 N on the Moon

award.4: four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: Her mass stays the same throughout, because she is made of the same amount of stuff. Her weight is the force of gravity on her, and weight = mass × gravitational field strength. As she flies away from Earth, Earth's pull gets weaker, so her weight falls; far out between the Earth and the Moon it is almost zero. As she nears the Moon, the Moon's gravity pulls on her more. On the Moon g is 1.6 N/kg instead of 10 N/kg, so her weight is about a sixth of what it was: if her mass is 60 kg, she weighs 600 N on Earth but only 96 N on the Moon.

questions.tip: Deal with mass and weight separately, use the formula, and follow her the whole way.

topics.title: Gravity, orbits and force diagrams
topics.summary: Every mass pulls on every other mass: how gravity depends on mass and distance, keeps moons and planets in orbit, and is drawn on force diagrams.

images.caption: Force diagrams: arrows show which way each force acts, and longer arrows mean bigger forces.
Gravitational field strength on the surface (or cloud tops) around the Solar System.

facts: **Gravity** is a **non-contact force**: it acts **without touching**, even across empty space.
**Every object with mass attracts every other object.** Gravity always **pulls (attracts)** — it never pushes.
The pull is **stronger** when the masses are **bigger**, and **weaker** when the objects are **further apart**.
Between everyday objects the pull is far too tiny to notice; you only notice it from something huge, like the Earth.
A **field** is the area where an object feels a force. Earth has a **gravitational field** around it, which gets weaker further out.
**Gravity holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth** and the **planets in orbit around the Sun**. Without it they would fly off in a straight line.
**Force diagrams:** each force is an **arrow** — the **direction** shows which way it acts, the **length** shows how big it is. **Weight** is drawn **straight down** from the middle of the object.
Unlike friction or air resistance, gravity needs no contact; unlike magnetism, it acts on **all** objects and **only attracts**.
For space missions: g is different on every planet, so astronauts' weight, how high they can jump and how much fuel a rocket needs to take off all change.
keywords: the force of attraction between any two masses
a force that acts without the objects touching
the area where other objects feel a force (here, gravitational)
the curved path of one object around another
a drawing with arrows showing the forces on an object
the upward push from a surface (normal contact force)

questions.answer: the Sun's gravity is weaker further away

questions.explain: Gravity weakens with distance, so the Sun pulls more gently on distant planets and they travel more slowly in their orbits.

questions.stem: Explain why the Moon keeps going round the Earth instead of flying off into space.

the pull acts towards the centre of the Earth

the pull keeps changing the Moon's direction, bending its path into a loop / orbit

markScheme.modelAnswer: The Moon is moving very fast, and on its own it would travel off in a straight line. But the Earth's gravity pulls on the Moon, towards the centre of the Earth. This pull keeps changing the Moon's direction, so its path is bent into an orbit around the Earth.

topics.title: Potential difference (voltage)
topics.summary: What potential difference is, how to measure it, and how it is shared in series but the same in parallel.

images.caption: Two identical lamps on a 6 V battery: in series they share it (3 V each), in parallel each gets all 6 V.

facts: **Potential difference** (also called **voltage**) is the push that drives charge round a circuit. It is measured in **volts (V)**.
Thinking in energy: potential difference tells you **how much energy each bit of charge carries** — energy it is given at the battery, and energy it hands over to a component such as a lamp.
Measure it with a **voltmeter** connected **in parallel** — across the component, on a little loop of its own, not in the main loop.
A battery's **rating** (6 V, 9 V…) is the size of its push. A bigger rating means more current and brighter lamps. A lamp is also rated: a 12 V lamp on a 6 V battery glows dimly.
In a **series** circuit the battery's potential difference is **shared** between the components: two identical lamps on 6 V get **3 V each**. The shares always **add up** to the battery's value.
In a **parallel** circuit every branch gets the **full** potential difference of the battery: two lamps on 6 V get **6 V each**, so they are brighter than in series.

**Why?** Each charge picks up energy at the battery and gives it all away before it gets back. In series it passes through **both** lamps, so its energy is split between them; in parallel it passes through **only one** lamp, which gets all of it.
In series, a component with a **bigger resistance** takes a **bigger share** of the potential difference — more energy is transferred there.
keywords: the push on the charge; energy carried by each bit of charge, in volts (V)
meter that measures potential difference, connected in parallel
on a separate loop — across a component
the voltage a battery gives, or a lamp is made for
in series, the components split the battery's voltage between them

questions.stem: What is the unit of potential difference?
questions.explain: Potential difference (voltage) is measured in volts, V.

questions.stem: What is another name for potential difference?
questions.explain: Potential difference and voltage mean the same thing.

questions.stem: Which meter measures potential difference?
questions.explain: A voltmeter (circle with a V) measures potential difference in volts.

questions.stem: Is a voltmeter connected in series or in parallel with the component it measures?
questions.explain: A voltmeter goes across the component, on its own loop — in parallel — so it can compare the two ends.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of potential difference?

how hard it is for charge to get through a component
the number of electrons in the wire
questions.explain: Potential difference is the push — the energy given to or passed on by each bit of charge. Charge per second is current; how hard it is to get through is resistance.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are in series with a 6 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp, in volts?
questions.explain: In series the 6 V is shared. Identical lamps share it equally: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 V each.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are in parallel with a 6 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp, in volts?
questions.explain: In parallel each branch gets the full potential difference of the battery: 6 V each.

questions.stem: A lamp and a buzzer are in series with a 9 V battery. The lamp has 4 V across it. What is the potential difference across the buzzer, in volts?
questions.explain: In series the shares add up to the battery's 9 V: 9 − 4 = 5 V.

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are in series with a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp, in volts?
questions.explain: The 12 V is shared equally between three identical lamps: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 V.

questions.stem: In a series circuit, the potential differences across the components add up to the potential difference of the battery.
questions.explain: True — the battery's voltage is shared out between the components in the loop.

questions.stem: In a parallel circuit, each branch gets only half of the battery's potential difference.
questions.explain: False — each branch gets the full potential difference of the battery.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are joined to the same battery, first in series and then in parallel. When are they brighter?
questions.answer: in parallel, because each lamp gets the full potential difference
choices: in series, because the current goes through both lamps
the same both times, because it is the same battery
in series, because the lamps share the energy
questions.explain: In parallel each lamp gets the whole battery voltage, so more energy goes to each lamp and they glow brighter.

questions.stem: Why does each of two identical lamps in series get half of the battery's potential difference?
questions.answer: each charge passes through both lamps, so its energy is split between them
choices: each lamp uses up half of the current
the current is halved before it reaches the second lamp
the battery only pushes charge as far as the first lamp
questions.explain: Every charge goes through both lamps on its way round, so the energy it carries is shared between them. The current is the same in both lamps.

questions.stem: The 1.5 V cell in a torch is swapped for a 3 V battery, with the same bulb. What happens?
questions.answer: the bulb is brighter, because the bigger push makes more current flow

nothing changes, because it is the same bulb
the bulb is brighter, but the current is smaller
questions.explain: A higher rating means a bigger push, so more current flows and more energy reaches the bulb each second.

questions.stem: A lamp made for 12 V is put in a circuit with a 6 V battery. How does it glow, compared with a 6 V lamp on the same battery?
questions.answer: more dimly, because it gets less potential difference than it was made for
choices: more brightly, because it is a bigger lamp
the same, because the battery is the same
it blows, because 12 is bigger than 6
questions.explain: The lamp is rated for 12 V, so with only 6 V it gets less energy than it needs to glow fully.

questions.stem: A lamp and a resistor with a bigger resistance are in series. Which gets the bigger share of the potential difference?

choices: the lamp, because it gives out light
they always get exactly half each
questions.explain: In series, the component with the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the voltage — more energy is transferred there.

questions.stem: In this circuit, which meter is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: A circle with V is a voltmeter. It sits across the lamp, in parallel.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are joined to a 6 V battery in series. Then they are joined to the same battery in parallel. Use ideas about energy to explain why the lamps are brighter in parallel.

acceptablePoints.point: in series the 6 V is shared, so each lamp gets 3 V (half)
in parallel each lamp gets the full 6 V
potential difference is the energy carried by each bit of charge: in series each charge gives its energy to both lamps, in parallel it gives all of it to one lamp
so each lamp in parallel gets more energy (each second) and glows brighter

award.3: one mark for each point, up to 3

markScheme.modelAnswer: In series the 6 V is shared, so each lamp only gets 3 V. In parallel each lamp gets the full 6 V. The potential difference is the energy carried by each bit of charge: in series a charge has to share its energy between both lamps, but in parallel it goes through only one lamp and gives it all its energy. So each lamp gets more energy and is brighter in parallel.

topics.title: Resistance, conductors and insulators
topics.summary: What resistance is, why conductors and insulators behave differently, and the water-pipe model of a circuit.

images.caption: The water-pipe model: the pump is the battery, the flow is the current, a narrow pipe is a high resistance.

facts: **Resistance** is how hard it is for charge to get through something. It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**.
A component with resistance **reduces the current** and **transfers energy to the surroundings**, mostly by **heating** (a lamp also gives out light).
**Electrical conductors** let charge through easily: they have a **low resistance** — metals such as copper, aluminium and steel, and also graphite.
**Electrical insulators** hardly let charge through at all: they have a **high resistance** — plastic, rubber, wood, glass and dry air.
A wire is **copper** inside a **plastic** coat: the copper carries the current, the plastic keeps it away from your fingers.
**Water-pipe model:** the battery is a **pump**, the current is the **water flowing** round, and a resistance is a **narrow pipe** — it is harder to push water through, so less flows.
A **longer** or **thinner** wire has **more resistance** (like a longer or narrower pipe); a shorter, thicker wire has less.
With the same battery, **more resistance means less current**. Adding lamps in series adds resistance, so the current falls and the lamps get dimmer.
A **variable resistor** lets you change the resistance, and so the current — for example to dim a light or slow a motor.
keywords: how hard it is for charge to get through, in ohms (Ω)
lets current through easily; low resistance
does not let current through easily; high resistance
a component that adds a set resistance
a resistor whose resistance can be changed
a simpler picture (like water in pipes) that helps explain how something works

markScheme.modelAnswer: In the model the battery is a pump that pushes water round the pipes, and the flow of water is the current. A high resistance is like a narrow section of pipe. topics.title: Calculating resistance
topics.summary: Working out resistance from potential difference and current, reading a results table, and what the numbers mean for safety.
facts: **Resistance (Ω) = potential difference (V) ÷ current (A).**
Example: a lamp has **12 V** across it and **2 A** through it. Resistance = 12 ÷ 2 = **6 Ω**.
To measure it: put an **ammeter in series** with the component and a **voltmeter across it** (in parallel). Read both, then divide the voltage by the current.
From a table of voltage and current, divide V by I for each row. If the answer stays the same (as for a resistor), the resistance is constant.
If V ÷ I changes, the resistance is changing — a lamp's thin filament gets **hotter** as the current rises, and its resistance goes **up**.
With the same potential difference, a **bigger resistance** means a **smaller current**.

**Safety:** your body has resistance. Dry skin has a high resistance; **wet skin** has a much lower one, so the same voltage pushes a much bigger, more dangerous current through you. Higher voltages (like the 230 V mains) are more dangerous too.

topics.title: Circuit symbols and diagrams
topics.summary: The symbols in circuit diagrams, where ammeters and voltmeters go, and turning diagrams into real circuits and back.

images.caption: Circuit symbols.
A series circuit: the ammeter is in the loop, the voltmeter is across a lamp.

facts: Circuit diagrams use **symbols** so anyone can draw and read them. Draw wires as **straight lines with a ruler**, with square corners.
**Cell:** a long thin line (the **+** side) and a short thick line (the **−** side). A **battery** is **two or more cells** joined together.
**Lamp:** a circle with a cross. **Switch:** a hinged line — when it is **open** there is a gap, so no current flows.
**Resistor:** a rectangle. **Variable resistor:** a rectangle with an arrow through it.
**Ammeter** (circle with **A**) measures current. It goes **in series** — in the main loop, so the current flows through it.
**Voltmeter** (circle with **V**) measures potential difference. It goes **in parallel** — across the component.
**In series:** components on the **same loop**, one after another. **In parallel:** components on **separate loops** (branches).
Current only flows round a **complete circuit** — a loop with no gaps.
**From diagram to real circuit:** start at the battery and follow the loop with your finger, joining each part in order. For a parallel circuit, build the main loop first, then add each branch.

two or more cells joined together

topics.title: Current in series and parallel
topics.summary: What current is, why it is the same everywhere in series, how it splits and joins in parallel, and when to use each.

images.caption: In a parallel circuit the current splits at a junction: 0.4 A + 0.2 A = 0.6 A in the main wire.

facts: **Current** is the flow of electric **charge** round a circuit. It is measured in **amperes (amps, A)** with an **ammeter**.

In metal wires the charge is carried by **electrons** — tiny particles in atoms with a **negative** charge. They are in the wire all the time; the battery pushes them all round at once, so a lamp lights straight away.
Current is **not used up**. As much charge comes back to the battery as leaves it — it is the **energy** that is passed on to the lamps.
**Series:** the current is the **same everywhere** in the loop. Adding more lamps in series makes the current smaller, and all the lamps dimmer.
**Parallel:** the current **splits** at a **junction** and **joins up** again where the branches meet. The branch currents **add up** to the current in the main wire.
Adding another branch in parallel makes the **total** current from the battery bigger; the lamps already there stay just as bright (but the battery runs down sooner).
**Series — good for:** simple circuits where one switch controls everything. **But** if one lamp breaks, the loop is broken and **everything goes off**.
**Parallel — good for:** house lighting and sockets. Each branch can have **its own switch**, every lamp gets the full voltage, and if one breaks **the others stay on**.

**Which way?** Electrons are negative, so they flow out of the battery's **negative** terminal, round the circuit and back into the **positive** one. Before electrons were known, scientists chose **+ to −** for current (**conventional current**) — circuit arrows still point that way.
keywords: the flow of electric charge, in amps (A)
the unit of current, usually shortened to amp
what flows in a current; electrons carry negative charge
tiny negatively charged particle, part of an atom
a point where a circuit splits into branches or they join
one of the separate loops in a parallel circuit
on the same loop: same current everywhere

series: the battery's voltage is shared between the lamps, so with many lamps each is dim (more lamps = more resistance, less current)

markScheme.modelAnswer: In series there is only one loop, so the same current flows through every lamp. The battery's voltage is shared between all the lamps, so with lots of lamps each one is dim. If one lamp breaks, the loop is broken and they all go out. In parallel each lamp is on its own branch: the current splits at the junctions and the branch currents add up to the total. Each lamp gets the full voltage, so they are brighter, and if one breaks the others stay on because their loops are still complete. But the parallel circuit takes more current, so the battery runs down sooner. Parallel is better if you want the lights to keep working; series is simpler.

topics.title: Static charge and electric fields
topics.summary: How rubbing charges things up, why charges attract or repel, electric fields, and how to avoid static shocks.

images.caption: Rubbing moves electrons from the jumper onto the balloon.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

facts: Atoms contain tiny **electrons**, which carry a **negative** charge. When two materials are **rubbed together**, electrons can move from one surface to the other: both get **charged up**.
The object that **gains electrons** becomes **negatively charged**. The object that **loses electrons** becomes **positively charged** — by the same amount.
**Only electrons move.** The positive charges stay put, deep inside the atoms.
**Like charges repel** (+ and +, − and −). **Unlike (opposite) charges attract** (+ and −).
Charged objects push or pull each other **without touching**: this is the **electrostatic force**, a **non-contact force**.
The space around a charged object where another charged object feels this force is its **electric field**. The field is **strongest close to** the object and gets **weaker further away**.
A charged comb or balloon can also pull small **uncharged** things, like bits of paper or hair, towards it.
A **static shock** happens when charge that has built up on you jumps to a metal object or the ground as a tiny spark.

**Fewer shocks:** wear **cotton** rather than nylon or wool, don't shuffle across nylon carpets, keep the air less dry, and touch metal with a **key** or let charge flow away gradually (anti-static wrist straps and mats do this).

topics.title: Energy resources
topics.summary: Where our electricity comes from: renewable and non-renewable resources, and how a power station works.

images.caption: A fuel-burning power station: the fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, the turbine turns a generator, and power lines carry the electricity to homes.

table.title: Some energy resources
head: Resource
Renewable?
Good points
Bad points
rows: Reliable; can be turned up when more electricity is needed
Give off carbon dioxide (climate change); will run out
No carbon dioxide while running; lots of energy from a little fuel

facts: An **energy resource** is anything with stored energy that we can release in a useful way — a fuel, the wind, moving water or sunlight.
**Fossil fuels** — **coal**, **crude oil** and **natural gas** — formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals that lived long ago.
**Non-renewable** resources cannot be replaced, so they will run out one day: the fossil fuels and **nuclear** fuel (uranium).

**Renewable** resources are replaced naturally and will not run out: **solar**, **wind**, **waves**, **tides**, **hydroelectric** (water falling from a dam), **geothermal** (heat from hot rocks underground) and **biomass** (wood, crops, animal waste).

In most power stations a **fuel** is burned to **boil water**. The **steam** spins a **turbine**, the turbine turns a **generator**, and the generator makes the electricity. **Power lines** (the National Grid) carry it to our homes.
Wind, wave, tidal and hydroelectric power stations turn the turbine **directly**, with no fuel and no boiler. **Solar cells** turn light straight into electricity.
Burning fossil fuels gives off **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that adds to **climate change**. Burning coal also gives off gases that cause **acid rain**.
Every resource has **advantages and disadvantages**, so the UK uses a **mix**: gas power stations can be turned up quickly when everyone puts the kettle on, but wind and solar depend on the weather.

When **demand** for electricity rises, a country can build more power stations (ideally renewable), store energy for calm, dark days, and help people **use less** — better insulation and more efficient devices.

markScheme.modelAnswer: A wind farm uses a renewable resource, so it will never run out, and it gives off no carbon dioxide while running; there is also no fuel to pay for. A gas power station is reliable and can be turned up quickly when demand rises, but gas is a non-renewable fossil fuel that will run out, it must be bought, and burning it gives off carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change. topics.title: Paying for electricity
topics.summary: Power, kilowatt-hours and how to work out what a device costs to run.

table.title: Typical powers of devices at home
head: Device
Power in W
Power in kW

facts: **Power** is how quickly a device transfers energy. It is measured in **watts (W)**. A 2000 W heater transfers 2000 joules every second — twice as fast as a 1000 W heater.
**1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.** To change watts into kilowatts, divide by 1000: 60 W = 0.06 kW.
We pay for electricity by the **amount of energy** we use, measured in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**. 1 kWh is the energy a 1 kW device transfers in 1 hour. Bills call it a **unit**.
**Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours).** Change minutes into hours first: 30 minutes = 0.5 h, 6 minutes = 0.1 h.
**Cost = power (kW) × time (hours) × price per kWh.** A 2 kW heater for 3 hours at 25p per kWh: 2 × 3 × 25 = **150p = £1.50**.
Devices that **heat** things — showers, kettles, heaters, ovens, tumble dryers — have the highest powers, so they cost the most to run.
**Filament bulbs** waste most of their energy heating the surroundings. **Fluorescent** (energy-saving) and **LED** bulbs give the same light for a much smaller power, so they are far cheaper to run.
A meter counts the kWh used. **Units used = new reading − old reading.**
To cut a bill: switch devices off rather than leaving them on **standby**, use LED bulbs, take shorter showers, boil only the water you need, dry clothes outside, and turn the heating down a degree.

the unit of power: 1 joule every second

topics.title: Energy in food and activities
topics.summary: Reading the energy on food labels in kilojoules, and comparing the energy different activities use.

images.caption: A food label gives the energy per 100 g and per portion, in kilojoules (kJ) and kilocalories (kcal).

table.title: Energy an adult transfers in different activities (rough figures)
head: Activity
kJ per minute

facts: Food is a **store of energy** — a **chemical store**. Your body releases the energy in **respiration**.
The unit of energy is the **joule (J)**. **1 kilojoule (kJ) = 1000 J.**
**Food labels** give the energy in food in **kilojoules (kJ)**, usually with **kilocalories (kcal)** beside it.
Labels show energy **per 100 g**, so you can compare foods fairly, and **per portion**, so you know what you actually eat.
Fatty foods store the most energy: a gram of **fat** holds about twice as much as a gram of carbohydrate or protein.
The more active you are, the more energy you transfer each minute: **running** uses several times as much as **sitting**.
Even asleep your body needs energy to keep your **heart beating**, to **breathe** and to **keep warm** (about 37 °C).
If you take in **more** energy than you use, the body stores the extra as **fat**; if you take in **less**, it uses up its stores.
UK labels compare food with an adult's **reference intake** of 8400 kJ a day. Growing teenagers and very active people need more.

topics.title: Energy stores
topics.summary: The energy stores that fill and empty when something happens — thermal, chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic.

images.caption: Five everyday examples, each with energy in a different store.

table.title: Energy stores
head: Store
Filled when…
Example
rows: (emptied when a chemical reaction transfers energy to the surroundings)
a book on a high shelf
a material is stretched or squashed
a stretched elastic band, a squashed spring

facts: We explain how jobs get done with an **energy model**: energy is in a **store** at the start, and is **transferred** to another store by the end.
**Thermal store** — filled when an object **warms up**. The hotter it is, the more energy in this store.
**Chemical store** — in **food, fuels and batteries**. It empties during **chemical reactions** (burning, respiration) as energy is transferred to the surroundings.
**Kinetic store** — any **moving** object. It fills when the object **speeds up**: the faster it goes, the more energy.
**Gravitational potential store** — filled when an object is **lifted higher**. The higher (and heavier) it is, the more energy.
**Elastic store** — filled when a material is **stretched or squashed (compressed)**. The more it is stretched or squashed, the more energy.
There are a few more stores you will meet later (nuclear, magnetic, electrostatic).
**Light, sound and electricity are NOT stores** — they are ways of **transferring** energy from one store to another.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**.

topics.title: Energy transfers
topics.summary: How energy moves from one store to another — mechanically, electrically, by heating and by light or sound — for example in a hand-crank torch.

images.caption: A hand-crank (wind-up) torch, cut open to show the generator, the rechargeable battery and the LED.

table.title: Describing a transfer: store → how → store
head: What happens
Store emptied
How
Store filled

facts: Energy moves between stores in four main ways: **mechanically** (a force moves something), **electrically** (an electric current), **by heating** (from hotter to cooler), and **by radiation** — **light** and **sound**.
Describe any change as **store at the start → how → store at the end**: kicking a ball is chemical store of your muscles → mechanically → kinetic store of the ball.
**Conservation of energy:** energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred. The **total** at the end is the same as at the start.

**Hand-crank torch:** the chemical store of your **muscles** empties as you turn the **handle** (mechanically) → the **generator** spins (kinetic store) → it transfers energy **electrically** to the **chemical store of the rechargeable battery**.

When the torch is switched on, the battery transfers energy **electrically** to the **LED**, which gives out **light** — the useful part. Some energy always **heats** the parts and the surroundings, and turning the gears makes a little **sound**.
A falling object: its **gravitational potential** store empties and its **kinetic** store fills.
Burning a fuel: the **chemical** store of the fuel empties and energy is transferred **by heating** to the **thermal** store of whatever is heated.
A **generator** transfers energy from a spinning (kinetic) store electrically; a **motor** does the opposite.

transferred by light or sound waves

topics.title: Wasted energy
topics.summary: Why some energy is always dissipated, how to work out useful and wasted energy, and why a pendulum or bouncing ball cannot go on for ever.

images.caption: A Sankey diagram: the width of each arrow shows how much energy goes that way.

table.title: Roughly how much of the input each source wastes
head: Energy source
Useful (electricity)
Wasted

facts: In every energy transfer, some energy spreads out into the surroundings in ways that are not useful. We say it is **dissipated** (wasted). It usually ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**, warming them very slightly.
Energy is **conserved**: **energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy**.
So **useful energy = energy in − wasted energy**, and **wasted energy = energy in − useful energy**.
Dissipated energy is spread so thinly that it is very hard to use again.
Much of the waste comes from **friction** and **air resistance**, which warm the moving parts and the air, and from **sound**.
A **Sankey diagram** shows energy transfers as arrows. The **width** of an arrow shows the amount; useful energy goes straight on, wasted energy bends away.
**Efficiency** = useful energy out ÷ energy in × 100%. A filament bulb turns only about 10% of its energy into light; an LED wastes much less.

A **swinging pendulum** or a **bouncing ball** cannot go on for ever: at every swing or bounce some energy is dissipated by air resistance, friction and sound, so it rises a little less each time until it stops.

We can waste less by **oiling (lubricating)** moving parts to cut friction, **streamlining** to cut air resistance, and **insulating** to cut heating losses. Renewable sources waste energy too — compare their percentages.
