questions.explain: The LED wastes much less energy heating the surroundings, so it needs less energy for the same light.

questions.stem: Which analogy best fits the energy model?
questions.answer: energy is like money moved between bank accounts — it moves around, but the total stays the same
choices: energy is like petrol — once it is burned it no longer exists
energy is like a liquid that gets used up as a job is done
energy is like a ball that is thrown away and lost
questions.explain: Like money moved between accounts, energy moves between stores but is never created or destroyed.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped onto the floor. Explain, in terms of energy, why it cannot keep bouncing for ever.

acceptablePoints.point: as the ball falls, its gravitational potential store empties and its kinetic store fills (and the reverse on the way up)
at each bounce, some energy is dissipated by sound and by heating the ball and floor
air resistance dissipates energy as the ball moves through the air
so less energy is left in the ball's stores each time, it rises less high, and in the end it stops
the energy is not destroyed — it ends up spread out in the thermal store of the surroundings

award.3: three points, including that energy is dissipated at each bounce

markScheme.modelAnswer: As the ball falls, energy moves from its gravitational potential store to its kinetic store. Each time it hits the floor, some energy is dissipated by sound and by heating the ball and the floor, and air resistance warms the air as it moves. So each bounce leaves the ball with less energy, it cannot rise as high, and finally it stops. The energy has not been destroyed — it has spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings.

questions.tip: Say where the energy goes at each bounce, and why that makes the next bounce lower.

topics.title: How sound travels
topics.summary: Sound is a vibration passed on by particles, so it needs a material to travel through and can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.

images.caption: A loudspeaker pushes and pulls on the air: the particles crowd together (compressions) and spread apart (rarefactions) as the wave moves on.

facts: Every sound starts with something **vibrating**: moving back and forth again and again (a guitar string, a drum skin, your vocal cords).

The vibration is passed from particle to particle as a **longitudinal wave**: the particles vibrate **in the same direction** as the wave travels. Where they crowd together is a **compression**; where they spread out is a **rarefaction**.
Sound needs **particles** to carry it, so it **cannot travel through a vacuum** (empty space with no particles). In space, nobody can hear you shout.
Sound travels **faster in denser materials**: fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases. In air it travels at about **330 m/s**.
Light is about **a million times faster** than sound. That is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.
When sound meets a surface it can be **reflected** (bounce back), **absorbed** (its energy goes into the material) or **transmitted** (pass through).
An **echo** is sound reflected back to the listener. Hard, flat surfaces give strong echoes; soft materials like foam, curtains and carpet **absorb** sound.
**Distance = speed × time.** For an echo, the sound goes there **and back**, so halve the total distance to find how far away the wall is.
keywords: a back and forth movement that repeats
a wave where the particles vibrate in the same direction as the wave travels
part of a sound wave where particles are squashed together
part of a sound wave where particles are spread apart
the material a wave travels through
a space with no particles at all
a sound reflected from a surface back to the listener
when a material takes in the energy of the sound
when sound passes through a material

questions.stem: Every sound is made by something moving quickly back and forth. What is this movement called?
questions.explain: A sound source vibrates: it moves back and forth again and again, pushing on the particles around it.

questions.stem: Sound travels as which type of wave?
questions.explain: In a sound wave the particles vibrate along the same line the wave travels, so it is a longitudinal wave.

questions.stem: In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate in which direction compared with the way the wave travels?
questions.explain: Longitudinal means the vibration is in the same direction as the wave moves: the particles move back and forth along it.

questions.stem: In a sound wave, what is a region where the particles are squashed close together called?
questions.explain: Compressions are where the particles crowd together; rarefactions are where they are spread apart.

questions.stem: Sound can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explain: A vacuum has no particles, so there is nothing to pass the vibrations on. Sound cannot travel through it.

questions.stem: What is a space with no particles of matter in it called?
questions.explain: A vacuum is completely empty: no particles at all, so sound cannot cross it (but light can).

questions.stem: Two astronauts on a spacewalk cannot hear each other shout, even when close together. Why?
questions.answer: space is a vacuum, so there are no particles to pass the vibrations on
choices: it is too cold in space for sound to form
sound travels too fast in space to be heard
their voices are too high-pitched in space
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium. With no particles between them, the vibrations from one astronaut cannot reach the other (they use radio, which can cross a vacuum).

questions.stem: Through which of these does sound travel fastest?
questions.explain: Sound is fastest in solids, where the particles are packed closely and pass vibrations on quickly. It cannot travel through a vacuum at all.

questions.stem: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
questions.explain: Water is denser than air: sound travels at about 1500 m/s in water and about 330 m/s in air.

questions.stem: Roughly how fast does sound travel in air, in metres per second?
questions.explain: Sound travels at about 330 m/s in air (some books say 340 m/s). Light is about a million times faster.

questions.stem: In a storm, why do you see the lightning before you hear the thunder?
questions.answer: light travels much faster than sound
choices: the lightning happens first and the thunder later
your eyes work faster than your ears
questions.explain: Both are made at the same moment, but light arrives almost instantly while sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 km.

questions.stem: You hear thunder 3 seconds after you see the lightning. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the storm, in metres?
questions.explain: Distance = speed × time = 330 × 3 = 990 m (the light reaches you almost instantly).

questions.stem: What is a sound reflected from a surface back to the listener called?
questions.explain: An echo is reflected sound. You hear it a moment later because the sound has travelled to the surface and back.

questions.stem: You shout towards a cliff and hear the echo 2 seconds later. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the cliff, in metres?
questions.explain: In 2 s the sound travels 330 × 2 = 660 m, but that is there and back, so the cliff is 660 ÷ 2 = 330 m away.

questions.stem: Which surface would give the clearest echo?
questions.explain: Hard, smooth surfaces reflect most of the sound. Soft materials absorb it, so there is little echo.

questions.stem: A music studio has foam on its walls. The sound's energy goes into the foam instead of bouncing back. The sound is…
questions.explain: Absorption: the sound's energy is transferred to the material, so less is reflected and the room has fewer echoes.

questions.stem: You can hear music from the next room through the wall. The sound has been…
questions.explain: Sound that passes through a material is transmitted. Walls transmit some sound, reflect some and absorb some.

questions.stem: A ringing electric bell is put inside a sealed glass jar. A pump slowly takes the air out of the jar. Describe and explain what you hear.

acceptablePoints.point: the sound gets quieter (and quieter) until it can hardly / no longer be heard
sound needs a medium / particles to travel through
as air is removed there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations
sound cannot travel through a vacuum (when the jar is empty)
you can still see the bell's hammer moving because light can travel through a vacuum

markScheme.modelAnswer: The ringing gets quieter and quieter until you can hardly hear it. Sound is a vibration passed on by particles. As the air is pumped out there are fewer particles to carry the vibrations, and sound cannot travel through a vacuum. You can still see the hammer hitting the bell because light does not need particles.

questions.stem: Explain why sound travels faster through a solid than through a gas.

acceptablePoints.point: the particles in a solid are closer together / packed tightly (it is denser)
so each particle passes the vibration on to the next more quickly
in a gas the particles are far apart, so the vibration takes longer to pass on

award.2: two points, linked (closer particles → vibrations passed on faster)

markScheme.modelAnswer: In a solid the particles are packed closely together, so a vibrating particle quickly bumps into the next one and passes the vibration on. In a gas the particles are far apart, so the vibrations are passed on more slowly.

topics.title: Loudness, pitch and oscilloscopes
topics.summary: The height of a sound wave shows how loud it is, and how many waves arrive each second shows its pitch.

images.caption: The parts of a wave: amplitude is measured from the middle line, wavelength from one crest to the next.
Oscilloscope traces with the same settings: taller waves are louder, more waves across the screen are higher in pitch.

facts: An **oscilloscope** shows a sound as a wavy line (a **trace**). A microphone first turns the sound into an electrical signal.
The **amplitude** is the biggest distance the wave moves from its **middle (rest) position**. **Bigger amplitude = louder sound.**
**Volume** (loudness) is measured in **decibels (dB)**.
The **frequency** is the number of waves each second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. **Higher frequency = higher pitch.**
The **wavelength** is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, such as **crest to crest**. A higher frequency means a **shorter wavelength**.
Loudness and pitch are separate: a sound can be **loud and low**, or **quiet and high**.
Comparing traces only works if the oscilloscope settings are the same. Count the waves across the screen for pitch; look at the height for loudness.
On an instrument: plucking or hitting **harder** makes a louder note (bigger amplitude); a **shorter, tighter or thinner** string makes a higher note (higher frequency).
keywords: the biggest distance a wave moves from its middle position
the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves
the number of waves each second, in hertz (Hz)
how high or low a sound is; set by the frequency
how loud or quiet a sound is, in decibels (dB)
a device that shows sound waves as a trace on a screen

questions.stem: What is the biggest distance a wave moves from its middle position called?
questions.explain: Amplitude is measured from the middle (rest) line to a crest or trough. A bigger amplitude means a louder sound.

questions.stem: What is the number of waves produced each second called?
questions.explain: Frequency is how many waves pass each second. It sets the pitch.

questions.stem: What unit is frequency measured in?
questions.explain: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is one wave each second.

questions.stem: What unit is the loudness (volume) of a sound measured in?
questions.explain: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Frequency is the one measured in hertz.

questions.stem: What is the distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest called?
questions.explain: Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves, such as crest to crest.

questions.stem: The pitch of a sound depends on which property of its wave?
questions.explain: Higher frequency means higher pitch. The amplitude sets the loudness, not the pitch.

questions.stem: A sound gets louder but stays the same pitch. What happens to its wave?
questions.explain: Louder means more energy and a bigger amplitude. The same pitch means the frequency has not changed.

questions.stem: A sound gets higher in pitch. What happens to its wave?
questions.answer: its frequency increases and its wavelength gets shorter
choices: its frequency decreases and its wavelength gets longer
questions.explain: Higher pitch means more waves each second, so each wave is shorter. Sound still travels at the same speed in air.

questions.stem: Which device shows a sound as a wavy trace on a screen (after a microphone has turned it into an electrical signal)?
questions.explain: An oscilloscope draws the electrical signal from a microphone, so you can see the sound's amplitude and frequency.

questions.stem: A high-pitched sound has a longer wavelength than a low-pitched sound.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: a higher pitch means a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength.

questions.stem: Two sounds can have the same pitch but different loudness.
questions.explain: Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude, so they can change separately (like a note played softly or loudly).

questions.stem: The four oscilloscope traces use the same settings. Which trace shows the highest-pitched sound?
questions.explain: C has the most waves across the screen, so it has the highest frequency and the highest pitch (even though it is quiet).

questions.stem: Which trace has the same pitch as A but is louder?
questions.explain: B has the same number of waves as A (same frequency) but they are much taller (bigger amplitude), so it is louder.

questions.stem: Which trace shows the quietest, lowest-pitched sound?
questions.explain: A has small waves (small amplitude, quiet) and only two waves across the screen (low frequency, low pitch).

questions.stem: Which trace is loud and has a higher pitch than B?
questions.explain: D is as tall as B (just as loud) but has more waves across the screen, so it has a higher frequency.

questions.stem: A guitarist plucks the same string again, but harder. How does the oscilloscope trace change?
questions.answer: the waves get taller, but the number of waves stays the same
choices: more waves fit across the screen
the waves get shorter and closer together
the trace does not change at all
questions.explain: Plucking harder gives a bigger amplitude (louder). The same string gives the same frequency, so the pitch stays the same.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The crest (or peak) is the highest point of a wave.

questions.stem: Which part of the wave is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The trough is the lowest point of a wave.

questions.stem: What does the arrow labelled {L} show?
questions.explain: The amplitude is measured from the middle line up to a crest (or down to a trough).

questions.stem: What does the arrow labelled {L} show?
questions.explain: The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next (or between any two matching points).

questions.stem: What is the dashed line labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The middle (rest) position is where the particles would be with no wave. The amplitude is measured from this line.

questions.stem: On the same oscilloscope settings, a quiet, low note and a loud, high note are shown. Describe how the two traces are different, and say what each difference tells you.

acceptablePoints.point: the loud note has taller waves / a bigger amplitude
a bigger amplitude means a louder sound
the high note has more waves across the screen / a higher frequency
a higher frequency means a higher pitch
the high note's waves are closer together / shorter wavelength

award.4: four points, covering both amplitude and frequency

markScheme.modelAnswer: The loud, high note has taller waves than the quiet note: a bigger amplitude, which means it is louder. It also has more waves across the screen, closer together: a higher frequency and shorter wavelength, which means a higher pitch. The quiet, low note has small waves that are spread out.

topics.title: Hearing and the ear
topics.summary: How the parts of the ear pass a sound on to the brain, what different animals can hear, and what can go wrong.

images.caption: Inside the ear: the vibration goes from the eardrum through three tiny bones to the cochlea, then the auditory nerve carries a signal to the brain.

table.title: The journey of a sound through the ear
head: Part
What it does
rows: collects sound and directs it into the ear canal
carries the sound to the eardrum
a thin skin that vibrates when sound hits it
three tiny bones that pass on the vibrations and make them bigger
a fluid-filled coil with tiny hairs that turn vibrations into electrical signals
carries the electrical signals to the brain

facts: The **outer ear (pinna)** collects sound waves and funnels them down the **ear canal**.
The sound makes the **eardrum** vibrate. Three tiny bones, the **ossicles**, pass the vibrations on and make them bigger.
In the **cochlea**, tiny **hair cells** turn the vibrations into **electrical signals**. The **auditory nerve** carries them to the **brain**, which makes sense of the sound.
The **auditory range** is the lowest to highest frequency an animal can hear. For a young human it is about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz**.
Sound too high for humans to hear is **ultrasound**. Dogs, cats and bats can hear some ultrasound; bats use it to find their way.
As people get older they usually **stop hearing the highest frequencies**.
**Very loud sounds** (over about 85 dB for a long time) can damage the hair cells in the cochlea. This **hearing loss is permanent**.
Other problems: a **perforated (burst) eardrum** cannot vibrate properly; **wax** blocking the ear canal stops sound reaching the eardrum. Both make sounds seem quieter.
**Ear defenders** and ear plugs protect hearing by **absorbing** sound energy, so less reaches the eardrum.
keywords: the part outside the head that collects sound
a thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it
three tiny bones that pass vibrations to the cochlea
coiled part of the inner ear where hair cells make electrical signals
carries signals from the cochlea to the brain
the lowest and highest frequencies an animal can hear
sound too high-pitched for humans to hear (above 20 000 Hz)

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The outer ear (pinna) is the part you can see. Its shape collects sound and funnels it into the ear canal.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The ear canal is the tube that carries sound from the outer ear to the eardrum.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The eardrum is a thin skin across the end of the ear canal. It vibrates when sound reaches it.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The ossicles are three tiny bones (hammer, anvil and stirrup) that pass the vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The cochlea is the snail-shaped coil. Its hair cells turn vibrations into electrical signals.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The auditory nerve carries electrical signals from the cochlea to the brain. (The optic nerve belongs to the eye.)

questions.stem: Which thin skin inside the ear vibrates when sound waves reach it?
questions.explain: Sound travels down the ear canal and makes the eardrum vibrate; the ossicles then pass the vibrations on.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear contains tiny hair cells that turn vibrations into electrical signals?
questions.explain: The hair cells in the fluid-filled cochlea move with the vibrations and send electrical signals along the auditory nerve.

questions.stem: In which order does a sound pass through the ear?
questions.answer: ear canal → eardrum → ossicles → cochlea → auditory nerve
choices: ear canal → cochlea → ossicles → eardrum → auditory nerve
eardrum → ear canal → cochlea → ossicles → auditory nerve
ear canal → ossicles → eardrum → auditory nerve → cochlea
questions.explain: Outside to inside: ear canal, eardrum, the three tiny bones, the cochlea, and then the nerve to the brain.

questions.stem: What is the name for the range from the lowest to the highest frequency an animal can hear?
questions.explain: The auditory range is different for different animals: dogs and bats can hear much higher frequencies than humans.

questions.stem: A young person can hear from about 20 Hz up to about how many hertz?
questions.explain: The human auditory range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, and the top end drops as people get older.

questions.stem: What is sound with a frequency too high for humans to hear called?
questions.explain: Ultrasound is above 20 000 Hz. (Infrasound is the opposite: below 20 Hz, too low for us.)

questions.stem: A dog can hear some high-pitched sounds that humans cannot.
questions.explain: A dog's auditory range goes much higher than ours, which is why dog whistles work even though we hear nothing.

questions.stem: As people get older, they usually lose the ability to hear the lowest-pitched sounds first.
questions.explain: It is the highest frequencies that go first as people age.

questions.stem: Years of very loud music can damage the tiny hair cells in the cochlea. What is the most likely effect?
questions.answer: permanent hearing loss, often of high-pitched sounds
choices: hearing gets better at high pitches
a short loss that always heals within a day
questions.explain: Damaged hair cells do not grow back, so the hearing loss is permanent. The cells for high frequencies are often damaged first.

questions.stem: A person has a perforated (burst) eardrum. Why can they not hear as well?
questions.answer: the eardrum cannot vibrate properly, so less vibration reaches the ossicles
choices: sound travels faster through the hole
the cochlea makes extra electrical signals
questions.explain: A hole in the eardrum means it does not vibrate properly, so sounds seem quieter. It usually heals by itself.

questions.stem: Ear defenders protect a road worker's hearing. How do they work?
questions.answer: they absorb sound energy, so less reaches the eardrum
choices: they change the sound into ultrasound
they make the sound travel faster
they reflect the sound back into the ear canal
questions.explain: Soft, thick materials absorb sound. Less sound reaches the eardrum, so the hair cells in the cochlea are not damaged.

questions.stem: Describe how the sound of a drum reaches your brain. Start with the drum skin being hit.

acceptablePoints.point: the drum skin vibrates
it makes the air particles next to it vibrate
the vibrations pass from particle to particle through the air as a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions)
the outer ear collects the sound and it travels down the ear canal
the eardrum vibrates
the ossicles / tiny bones pass on (and make bigger) the vibrations
hair cells in the cochlea turn the vibrations into electrical signals
the auditory nerve carries the signals to the brain

award.6: six points in a sensible order, from drum to brain
award.4: four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: When the drum is hit, its skin vibrates. This pushes and pulls on the air particles next to it, which vibrate and pass the vibration on to the next particles, so a longitudinal sound wave travels through the air. The outer ear collects the sound and it travels down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates. The ossicles pass these vibrations on and make them bigger. In the cochlea, tiny hair cells turn the vibrations into electrical signals, and the auditory nerve carries them to the brain.

questions.stem: A company says its new headphones "block out 95% of outside noise". Describe what evidence you would want to see before believing this claim.

acceptablePoints.point: measurements of the sound level in decibels with a sound meter, with and without the headphones
tests at a range of frequencies / both low- and high-pitched sounds (and different loudness)
a fair test: same sound source, same distance, only the headphones changed
repeated measurements / several pairs tested, so the results are reliable
tested by an independent group, not only by the company selling them

markScheme.modelAnswer: I would want measurements in decibels from a sound meter placed inside and outside the headphones, using the same sound source at the same distance. They should test low- and high-pitched sounds, because headphones often block high sounds better than low ones. The tests should be repeated and done by an independent group, not just the company.

topics.title: Light, shadows and mirrors
topics.summary: Light travels in straight lines, very fast; materials can transmit, absorb, reflect or scatter it, and mirrors reflect it at equal angles.

images.caption: Reflection in a plane mirror: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
A periscope: two mirrors at 45° each turn the light through a right angle.
Eclipses are shadows: of the Moon on the Earth (solar) or of the Earth on the Moon (lunar).

table.title: How much light gets through?
head: Type of material
Light through it
Examples
rows: all (or nearly all); you can see clearly through it
some, but scattered; you cannot see clearly through it

facts: Light travels in **straight lines**, at **300 million m/s** in a vacuum: nothing is faster. Unlike sound, it **can travel through a vacuum**.
Light **sources** (the Sun, a lamp) give out light. We see everything else because light **reflects** off it **into our eyes**.
When light meets a material it can be **transmitted** (pass through), **absorbed** (energy goes into the material), **reflected** or **scattered**. Usually a mix happens.
**Transparent** materials let all light through, **translucent** ones let some through, **opaque** ones let none through.
A **shadow** forms because light travels in straight lines and an opaque object blocks it. **Eclipses** are giant shadows.
A **smooth, shiny surface** like a mirror reflects all the rays the same way, so you see an image. A **rough** surface **scatters** light in all directions.
**Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.** Both are measured from the **normal**, a line at right angles (90°) to the mirror.
The image in a flat mirror is the **same size**, the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front, and **left-right reversed**.
In a **periscope**, two mirrors at **45°** each turn the light through 90°, so you can see over a wall.
keywords: the ray of light going towards a surface
the ray of light coming away from a surface
a line at right angles to the surface, used to measure angles
the angle between the incident ray and the normal
the angle between the reflected ray and the normal
lets some light through, but scattered
when the energy of light is taken in by a material
when light bounces off a surface in all directions

questions.stem: What is the dashed line labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The normal is drawn at right angles to the mirror where the ray hits it. Angles are measured from it.

questions.stem: Which ray is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The incident ray is the one travelling towards the mirror (look at the arrow).

questions.stem: Which ray is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The reflected ray is the one travelling away from the mirror after bouncing off it.

questions.stem: Which angle is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The angle of incidence is between the incident ray and the normal (not the mirror).

questions.stem: Which angle is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The angle of reflection is between the reflected ray and the normal. It always equals the angle of incidence.

questions.stem: What is labelled {L}?
questions.explain: The mirror is drawn as a line with short hatching on the back (the non-shiny side).

questions.stem: A ray of light hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection, in degrees?
questions.explain: The law of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 35°.

questions.stem: A ray hits a mirror at 30° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
questions.explain: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror: 90° − 30° = 60°.

questions.stem: How fast does light travel in a vacuum, in metres per second?
questions.explain: Light travels at 300 million m/s in a vacuum, about a million times faster than sound in air.

questions.stem: Light, like sound, cannot travel through a vacuum.
questions.explain: Light does not need particles, so it crosses the vacuum of space: that is how sunlight reaches us.

questions.stem: Frosted glass lets some light through but you cannot see clearly through it. It is…
questions.explain: Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it, so things look blurred.

questions.stem: A material that lets no light through at all is…
questions.explain: Opaque materials absorb or reflect all the light, which is why they make shadows.

questions.stem: Clear window glass lets almost all light through, so you can see clearly through it. It is…
questions.explain: Transparent materials transmit nearly all the light without scattering it.

questions.stem: This page does not give out its own light. Why can you see it?
questions.answer: light from a source reflects off the page into your eyes
choices: light travels from your eyes to the page
the page absorbs all the light that hits it
the page is a light source
questions.explain: We see objects that are not light sources because light reflects (scatters) off them and enters our eyes.

questions.stem: When light hits a rough surface and bounces off in all directions, this is called…
questions.explain: A rough surface scatters light in all directions, so you see the surface but no clear image in it.

questions.stem: Light shines on a sheet of white paper. What happens to most of the light?
questions.answer: it is scattered in all directions
choices: it is reflected as a clear image, like a mirror
questions.explain: Paper is opaque and its surface is rough on a tiny scale, so it scatters light. That is why you see the paper but not your face in it.

questions.stem: Which describes your image in a flat (plane) mirror?
questions.answer: the same size, as far behind the mirror as you are in front, and left-right reversed
choices: smaller than you, and on the surface of the mirror
upside down, and the same size
bigger than you, and in front of the mirror
questions.explain: A plane mirror gives an upright image, the same size, the same distance behind the mirror, with left and right swapped.

questions.stem: You stand 2 m in front of a flat mirror. How far are you from your image, in metres?
questions.explain: The image is 2 m behind the mirror and you are 2 m in front of it, so you are 2 + 2 = 4 m from your image.

questions.stem: In a periscope, each of the two mirrors is tilted at what angle, in degrees?
questions.explain: A mirror at 45° turns the light through 90°: once down the tube and once back out towards your eye.

questions.stem: In a solar eclipse, which object is between the Sun and the Earth?
questions.explain: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light and its shadow falls on part of the Earth.

questions.stem: During a solar eclipse, what do people standing in the darkest part of the Moon's shadow see?
questions.answer: a total eclipse: the Sun is completely blocked
choices: a partial eclipse: only part of the Sun is blocked
no eclipse: the Sun looks normal
a lunar eclipse: the Moon turns red
questions.explain: In the darkest shadow no direct sunlight arrives at all. Just outside it, in the paler shadow, people see part of the Sun covered (partial eclipse).

questions.stem: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
questions.answer: the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
choices: the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth, so the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
the Sun moves behind the Moon
the Moon stops reflecting light because it is new moon
questions.explain: In a lunar eclipse the Moon passes through Earth's shadow, so it goes dark (often a reddish colour).

questions.stem: Explain how a periscope lets you see over a wall. You may use the idea of rays.

acceptablePoints.point: light from the object travels in a straight line into the top of the periscope
the top mirror (at 45°) reflects the light down the tube / turns it through 90°
the bottom mirror (at 45°) reflects the light out into your eye
at each mirror the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (45°)

topics.title: Refraction, lenses and the eye
topics.summary: Light bends when it passes between materials; lenses use this to focus light, as the eye does onto the retina.

images.caption: Light through a glass block bends towards the normal on the way in and away from it on the way out.
A convex lens brings rays together at a focus; a concave lens spreads them out.
The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina; the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

table.title: Fixing blurred vision
head: Problem
What goes wrong
Lens that corrects it
rows: light focuses in front of the retina

facts: **Refraction** is the change in direction of light as it goes from one material into another. It happens because light **changes speed**.
Going into a **denser** material (air → glass or water), light slows down and bends **towards the normal**.
Going into a **less dense** material (glass or water → air), light speeds up and bends **away from the normal**.
A ray that hits the surface **along the normal** (at 90°) changes speed but **does not change direction**.
Refraction makes a pool look **shallower** than it is and a straw in a glass look **bent**: our brain assumes light travels in straight lines.
A **convex** lens is **thicker in the middle**. It brings rays together (**converges** them) at a point called the **focus**. Magnifying glasses are convex.
A **concave** lens is **thinner in the middle**. It spreads rays out (**diverges** them).

In the eye, the **cornea** and **lens** focus light onto the **retina**, which has light-detecting cells. The **optic nerve** carries signals to the **brain**. The **iris** changes the size of the **pupil** to let in more or less light.
**Short-sighted** eyes focus light in front of the retina: **concave** lenses fix it. **Long-sighted** eyes focus it behind the retina: **convex** lenses fix it.

topics.title: Colour
topics.summary: White light is a mixture of colours; objects and filters look coloured because of which colours they reflect, absorb or let through.

images.caption: A prism splits white light into a spectrum: red is bent least, violet most.

facts: **White light** is a mixture of all the colours. A **prism** splits it into a **spectrum**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. This is called **dispersion**.
Each colour is refracted by a different amount: **red the least, violet the most**, so the colours spread out.
Different colours of light have different **frequencies**: **red is the lowest**, **violet the highest**.
A coloured object **reflects** its own colour and **absorbs** the others. A red apple reflects red light and absorbs the rest.
**White** objects reflect all colours. **Black** objects absorb all colours.
In coloured light, an object looks its own colour only if that colour is in the light; otherwise it reflects nothing and looks **black**. A white object takes the colour of the light.
A **filter** **transmits** (lets through) only its own colour and **absorbs** the rest. A red filter does not add red: it takes the other colours away.
The **primary colours of light** are **red, green and blue**. Red + green = **yellow**, red + blue = **magenta**, green + blue = **cyan**, all three = **white**.

topics.title: Solids, liquids and gases
topics.summary: How the arrangement and movement of particles explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

images.caption: The same particles arranged as a solid, a liquid and a gas.

table.title: Comparing the three states
head: Solid
Liquid
Gas
rows: takes the shape of its container

facts: Everything is made of **particles** (atoms or molecules). They are far too small to see, even with a light microscope.

The **particle model** explains how a substance behaves from how its particles are **arranged** and how they **move**. A substance has the **same particles** in all three states — only the arrangement and movement change.
**Solid:** particles **touching** in a **regular pattern**, held in place, **vibrating on the spot**. So a solid keeps its shape, cannot flow and cannot be squashed.

**Liquid:** particles still **touching** but in **no pattern**, and they **slide past each other**. So a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, but hardly squashes — there are no gaps to push the particles into.
**Gas:** particles **far apart**, in no pattern, moving **fast in all directions**. So a gas spreads out to fill any container, flows, and is easy to **compress** (squash) because of the big spaces.

**Density** is how much mass there is in a certain volume — how closely packed the particles are. Solids and liquids are dense; gases have a very low density. (Ice is unusual: it is less dense than water, so it floats.)
When something is heated its particles **move or vibrate faster** and get a little **further apart**, so it **expands**. The particles themselves never get bigger, melt or change shape.

Some materials are tricky to classify. **Sand** pours like a liquid, but every grain is a solid with a fixed shape. **Toothpaste** and **jelly** keep their shape until pushed. Decide by asking what the particles of each part are doing.

topics.title: Changes of state
topics.summary: Melting, freezing, evaporating, boiling, condensing and subliming explained by particles gaining or losing energy.

images.caption: The changes of state. Red arrows: particles gain energy. Blue arrows: they lose energy.
Heating ice at a steady rate: the line is flat while the state changes.

table.title: The changes of state
head: Change
From → to
Particles
rows: liquid → gas, at the surface, any temperature
liquid → gas, all through the liquid, at the boiling point

facts: Changes of state are **physical changes**: the particles stay the same, no new substance is made, they can be reversed, and the **mass stays the same**.
**Heating** gives the particles more **energy**, so they move or vibrate faster. **Cooling** takes energy away, so they slow down.

**Melting** happens at the **melting point**: the particles vibrate so much that they break out of their fixed pattern. **Freezing** happens at the **same temperature**, when the particles lose energy and settle back into a pattern.

**Boiling** happens at the **boiling point**, with bubbles of gas forming all through the liquid. **Evaporating** happens only at the **surface**, at **any temperature** — the fastest particles escape. That is how puddles and washing dry.
**Condensing** is gas turning back into liquid when it cools — like mist on a cold bathroom mirror.
**Subliming** is a solid turning straight into a gas, e.g. **dry ice** (solid carbon dioxide) or iodine.

A substance is a **solid below its melting point**, a **liquid between** its melting and boiling points, and a **gas above its boiling point**. Water: melting point **0 °C**, boiling point **100 °C**.
On a **heating curve** the temperature stays **flat** while the substance melts or boils: the energy goes into freeing the particles, not into making them hotter.

topics.title: Diffusion and gas pressure
topics.summary: How moving particles spread out by themselves, and how their collisions with walls make gas pressure.

images.caption: Diffusion: perfume particles spread out among the air particles by themselves.
Gas pressure comes from particles hitting the walls of the container.

facts: **Diffusion**: particles of a liquid or gas spread out by their own **random movement**, from where there are **lots** of them (high concentration) to where there are **fewer** (low concentration). No stirring is needed.
Examples: the smell of perfume or cooking spreads across a room; a drop of ink slowly colours a glass of water; tea spreading from a tea bag.
Diffusion is **faster in gases** than in liquids (the particles move faster and have more space) and **faster when it is warmer**. It does not happen in solids, where particles cannot move about.
**Gas pressure** is caused by gas particles **colliding with the walls** of their container. Each hit gives a tiny push; all the pushes together make the pressure.

The pressure goes **up** when there are **more particles** in the same space (pumping up a tyre), when the gas is **squashed** into a smaller volume, or when it is **heated** (the particles move faster, so they hit the walls **harder and more often**).

That is why a balloon grows when you blow more air in, why an aerosol can must never be heated, and why a sealed crisp packet puffs up high on a mountain, where fewer air particles push on the outside.

**Evidence for particles:** smells spread (diffusion); gases can be squashed (there are spaces); sugar "disappears" in tea but the tea tastes sweet; under a microscope, specks of smoke or pollen **jiggle randomly** (**Brownian motion**) because invisible particles keep bumping into them.

topics.title: Pure substances, mixtures and solutions
topics.summary: What makes a substance pure, how things dissolve, how to read a solubility curve, and how to get a solid back by evaporating.

images.caption: A solubility curve: how much of solid X dissolves in 100 g of water at each temperature.
Evaporating the water from a salt solution.

facts: A **pure substance** is just one element or one compound, with nothing mixed in. It melts and boils at **fixed temperatures** (pure water: 0 °C and 100 °C).

A **mixture** is two or more substances mixed but not joined, so it can be separated using differences in their **physical properties**. It melts or boils over a **range** of temperatures. **Air, fruit juice, sea water and milk are all mixtures.** ("Pure orange juice" on a carton only means nothing was added.)

**Dissolving:** a **solute** (like sugar) mixes completely with a **solvent** (like water) to make a **solution**. The solvent particles pull the solute particles apart and they spread out in between. The solute is still there — you can taste it.
**Mass is conserved:** mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. 10 g of salt in 100 g of water makes 110 g of solution.

**Soluble** substances dissolve (salt, sugar in water); **insoluble** ones do not (sand, chalk). A solution is see-through, though it may be coloured. Dissolving is not melting: melting needs one substance and heat.
**Solubility** is the most solute that dissolves in a certain amount of solvent, often given in **g per 100 g of water**. When no more can dissolve, the solution is **saturated**.
For most solids, solubility **rises as the temperature rises**. A **solubility curve** shows this. Cool a hot saturated solution and the solid that no longer fits comes out as **crystals**.

**Evaporation** gets a dissolved solid back: heat the solution in an **evaporating basin** so the water turns to gas and the solid is left. For bigger crystals (**crystallisation**), heat until about half the water has gone, then leave it to cool.

topics.title: Filtration and distillation
topics.summary: Choosing a method to separate a mixture: filtering, evaporating, distilling or using a magnet.

images.caption: Filtration: the insoluble solid stays in the paper.
Simple distillation: boil, then condense the gas back into a pure liquid.

table.title: Which method?
head: Mixture
Method
Why it works
rows: insoluble solid in a liquid (sand and water)

facts: Choose the method from **how the substances are different**: grain size and solubility (filter), boiling point (evaporate, distil), how well they dissolve in a solvent (chromatography), magnetism (magnet).

**Filtration:** pour the mixture through **filter paper** in a **funnel**. The liquid and anything dissolved in it pass through as the **filtrate**; the insoluble solid stays behind as the **residue**.
Filtration cannot remove a **dissolved** solid: its particles are spread out among the water particles and pass straight through the paper.

**Simple distillation:** heat the solution until the liquid **boils**. The gas goes into the **condenser**, where cold water cools it so it **condenses**. The pure liquid (the **distillate**) drips into the collecting flask; dissolved solids stay in the flask.

**Cold water goes in at the bottom** of the condenser and out at the top, so the cooling jacket stays completely full. The **thermometer bulb** sits level with the side arm to measure the temperature of the gas leaving.
Liquids have **different boiling points** (ethanol 78 °C, water 100 °C), so distillation can also separate two liquids: the one with the **lower boiling point** boils off first.

Complicated mixtures need **several steps**. **Rock salt** (salt + sand and grit): crush it, stir it into warm water so the salt dissolves, **filter** off the sand, then **evaporate** the filtrate to get salt crystals.
**Safety:** wear eye protection, heat gently, and don't boil a solution dry — the solid can spit out.

topics.title: Chromatography
topics.summary: Separating the coloured substances in inks and dyes, and using the results to identify unknown substances.

images.caption: Paper chromatography: the solvent carries the dyes up the paper.
A chromatogram: three known dyes (A, B, C) and two unknown inks (X, Y).

facts: **Chromatography** separates the different **coloured substances** in a mixture, such as the dyes in an ink or a food colouring.

**Method:** draw a **baseline in pencil** about 1–2 cm from the bottom of the paper. Put a small spot of each sample on it. Stand the paper in a beaker with a little **solvent** (water or ethanol), with the solvent **below the baseline**. When the solvent has nearly reached the top, take the paper out, mark the **solvent front** and let it dry. The result is a **chromatogram**.
**How it works:** the solvent soaks up the paper and carries the dyes with it. Dyes that **dissolve better** in the solvent travel **further**, so the dyes spread out.
**Pencil**, because it does not dissolve — pen ink would run up the paper too. **Solvent below the baseline**, or the spots would wash off into the solvent instead of moving up.
A **pure** substance gives **one spot**; a mixture gives two or more. A spot that stays on the baseline is **insoluble** in that solvent.

**Identifying unknowns:** run known substances next to the unknown on the same paper. A spot at the **same height** as a known one is probably that substance. A spot that matches nothing is a substance you did not test.
**How sure can you be?** Two different substances can travel the same distance in one solvent. Repeating with a **different solvent** — and still getting a match — gives much stronger evidence.

the dried paper showing the separated spots

topics.title: Metals and non-metals
topics.summary: How to tell a metal from a non-metal by its properties, the odd ones out, and why we choose certain metals for certain jobs.

table.title: Typical properties
head: Property
Metals
Non-metals
rows: bromine is a liquid; graphite conducts

facts: **Metals** are usually **shiny**, **good conductors** of electricity and heat, **malleable** (hammer them into shape) and **ductile** (pull them into wires). Most are solid at room temperature with high melting points.
**Non-metals** are usually **dull**, **poor conductors** (insulators) and, if solid, **brittle** — they shatter when hit. Many are **gases** at room temperature, such as oxygen and nitrogen.
Only three elements are **magnetic**: **iron, nickel and cobalt**. Steel is magnetic because it is mostly iron. Most metals, like copper and aluminium, are **not** magnetic.
**Mercury** is the only metal that is a **liquid** at room temperature. **Bromine** is the only non-metal that is a **liquid** at room temperature.
**Graphite** (a form of carbon) is an unusual non-metal: it **conducts electricity**.
To identify an **unknown element**, look at several properties together: shiny + conducts + malleable → a metal; dull + brittle + does not conduct → a non-metal.

We choose a material for its properties: **copper** for wires (conducts well, ductile), **aluminium** for aircraft (light, does not corrode), **gold** for jewellery (shiny, unreactive), **iron/steel** for bridges (strong).
Most elements in the periodic table are metals. Metals are on the **left** and middle; non-metals are on the **right**.

topics.title: Reactions with oxygen
topics.summary: Oxidation: metals and non-metals join with oxygen to make oxides — metal oxides are bases, non-metal oxides are acidic.

images.caption: Particle pictures: the atoms are rearranged, never made or destroyed.

facts: **Oxidation** is a reaction where a substance **combines with oxygen**. **Burning** (combustion) is fast oxidation that gives out heat and light.
**Metal + oxygen → metal oxide.** Magnesium burns with a dazzling **white flame** and leaves a white powder, **magnesium oxide**.
**Non-metal + oxygen → non-metal oxide**, often a gas: carbon makes **carbon dioxide**, sulfur makes **sulfur dioxide**.
**Metal oxides are bases** — they neutralise acids. Those that dissolve in water make **alkaline** solutions.
**Non-metal oxides are acidic** — they dissolve in water to make **acidic** solutions. Sulfur dioxide from burning fuels causes **acid rain**.
Oxidation can be **slow**: **rusting** is iron reacting with oxygen and water. A shiny metal that turns **dull** or dark on the surface (tarnishing) has reacted with oxygen — a **chemical change**.
In a **particle diagram** the atoms are **rearranged**: none are made or destroyed. The oxide has **more mass** than the metal because oxygen atoms have joined it.
To write a **word equation**: reactants on the left, an arrow (→, meaning 'makes'), products on the right.

a compound of an element with oxygen
burning: fast oxidation that gives out heat and light
a substance that neutralises an acid

topics.title: The reactivity series and displacement
topics.summary: Metals in order of how readily they react: metals with acids make a salt and hydrogen, and a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

images.caption: The reactivity series: the higher up, the more readily the metal reacts.
Testing for hydrogen: a lit splint at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop.

table.title: Metals in dilute hydrochloric acid
head: Metal
What you see
Reactivity
rows: fizzes fast, gets warm, metal soon disappears

facts: **Reactivity** is how readily a substance reacts. The **reactivity series** lists metals from most to least reactive: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold.
**Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.** For example: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen.
**Test for hydrogen:** hold a **lit splint** at the mouth of the tube — hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop**.
The more reactive the metal, the **faster** it fizzes and the **warmer** the mixture gets. **Copper, silver and gold do not react** with dilute acids.
**Displacement:** a **more reactive** metal takes the place of a **less reactive** metal in its compound. zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.
If the metal added is **less reactive** than the one in the compound, **nothing happens** — copper in magnesium sulfate solution does not react.
To **order metals** by experiment: use the same size pieces and the same volume and concentration of acid, then compare how fast they bubble or how much the temperature rises.
An **unfamiliar metal** goes in the series by comparing it: if it reacts faster than zinc but slower than magnesium, it goes between them.
**Gold** is so unreactive that it is found in the ground as the pure metal, and it stays shiny for thousands of years.

topics.title: pH and indicators
topics.summary: The pH scale from 0 to 14, strong and weak acids, concentration, hazards, and indicators that tell acids from alkalis.

images.caption: The pH scale with the colours of universal indicator.

facts: The **pH scale** runs from **0 to 14**. **Acids** have a pH **below 7**, **neutral** solutions (like pure water) are **pH 7**, **alkalis** have a pH **above 7**.
The **lower** the pH, the **stronger** the acid. The **higher** the pH, the stronger the alkali.

**Strong acids:** hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid. **Weak acids:** acetic acid (also called ethanoic acid, in vinegar) and citric acid (in lemons). At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.

**Indicators** change colour to show whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. **Litmus** turns **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali. **Universal indicator** has many colours, so it shows the **pH number** (match it to a colour chart). A **pH probe** gives an exact reading.
To tell two solutions apart, choose an indicator that **changes colour between** their two pH values.
**Concentration** is how many particles are in a given volume. **Concentrated** means lots of acid particles in the water; **dilute** means few. Concentrated is **not** the same as strong.
Acids and alkalis can be **corrosive** (destroy skin and eyes) or **irritant** (make skin red and sore). Very low or very high pH, and high concentration, mean more danger: wear **eye protection**.

topics.title: Neutralisation
topics.summary: Acids and bases cancel each other out to make a salt and water — how to name the salt, make a neutral solution, and where we use it.

images.caption: Neutralising an acid: add alkali a little at a time and stir until the indicator turns green.

facts: A **base** is a substance that **neutralises** an acid. A base that **dissolves in water** is called an **alkali** (e.g. sodium hydroxide).
**Acid + alkali → salt + water.** This reaction is called **neutralisation**.

**Naming the salt:** the first word comes from the **metal** in the alkali or base; the second from the **acid** — hydrochloric → **chloride**, sulfuric → **sulfate**, nitric → **nitrate**. Potassium hydroxide + nitric acid → potassium nitrate + water.

**Making a neutral solution:** put a measured volume of acid in a beaker with a few drops of universal indicator; add alkali **a little at a time**, stirring; stop when the indicator turns **green** (pH 7). A **pH probe** makes this more accurate.
**Indigestion tablets** contain a base that neutralises extra **stomach acid**.
Farmers spread **lime** (a base) on **acidic soil**; lime is also added to lakes damaged by acid rain. Factory **acid waste** is neutralised before it goes into rivers.
**Toothpaste** is slightly alkaline: it neutralises acids made by bacteria in your mouth, which would damage your teeth.
To **compare indigestion remedies**, use the same volume of the same acid each time and find how much of each remedy it takes to reach pH 7 — the less needed, the better it works.

a substance that neutralises an acid
a base that dissolves in water

topics.title: Inside the Earth
topics.summary: The layers the Earth is made of, from the thin rocky crust to the solid inner core, and what rocks are made of.

images.caption: The layers of the Earth (not to scale).
images.title: Layers of the Earth

facts: The Earth is built in layers. The three rock layers are the **crust**, the **mantle** and the **core**.
**Crust** — the thin, solid, rocky outside that we live on. It is thinnest under the oceans (about 6 km) and thickest under mountains (up to about 70 km).
**Mantle** — the thickest layer, nearly 3000 km deep. It is very hot rock that is mostly solid but can **flow very slowly**, like extremely thick toffee.
**Core** — made mostly of the metals **iron and nickel**. The **outer core is liquid**; the **inner core is solid**, because the pressure there is so huge, even though it is the hottest part.
The deeper you go, the **hotter** it gets and the **higher the pressure**.
**Atmosphere** — the layer of gases around the Earth: about **78 % nitrogen**, **21 % oxygen**, and small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Rocks are made of **minerals** — natural chemicals, usually in the form of grains or crystals. Quartz and calcite are two common minerals.
Nobody has dug deeper than the crust. Scientists work out what is inside the Earth from the way **earthquake waves** travel through it.

topics.title: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
topics.summary: The three kinds of rock, how each one forms, and how the way it forms explains what it is like.

images.caption: Close up: how the crystals or grains fit together in each kind of rock.

table.title: The three kinds of rock
head: Kind
How it forms
What it is like
Examples
rows: magma or lava cools and crystallises
interlocking crystals; hard; no gaps; no fossils
layers of sediment are compacted and cemented
rounded grains with gaps (porous); often crumbly; layers (strata); may have fossils

facts: **Igneous rocks** form when **magma** (melted rock underground) or **lava** (melted rock at the surface) **cools and crystallises**. Examples: **granite, basalt, obsidian**.

**Cooling speed sets crystal size.** Magma cooling **slowly** deep underground gives crystals time to grow **large** (granite). Lava cooling **quickly** at the surface makes **small** crystals (basalt). Very fast cooling makes a **glass with no crystals** (obsidian).
Igneous crystals **interlock** with no gaps, so the rock is **hard** and does not soak up water.

**Sedimentary rocks** form from **layers of sediment** (bits of rock, sand, mud or shells). The layers are **compacted** (squeezed by the weight above) and **cemented** (glued by minerals left by water). Examples: **limestone, chalk, sandstone**.

Sedimentary rocks have **rounded grains with gaps**, so they are often **porous** (soak up water) and **crumbly**. They lie in layers called **strata** and can contain **fossils**. The **oldest layer is usually at the bottom** — it was laid down first.

**Metamorphic rocks** form when existing rock is changed by **heat and pressure** over a long time, **without melting**. **Limestone or chalk → marble**; **mudstone or shale → slate**; **schist** forms at even higher heat and pressure.
Metamorphic rocks are **hard**, with crystals often lined up in **bands**. Any fossils are squashed and usually destroyed.
Rocks are clues: rounded pebbles cemented in layers on **Mars** suggest **water once flowed** there; **basalt** means there were **volcanoes**.
**Pottery and bricks** are made by heating clay in a very hot kiln. Like a metamorphic rock, the clay **changes and hardens without melting**.

topics.title: Weathering, erosion and the rock cycle
topics.summary: How rocks are broken down, carried away and laid down, and how the rock cycle turns one kind of rock into another.

images.caption: The rock cycle: how one kind of rock becomes another.
images.title: The rock cycle

facts: **Weathering** is rock breaking down **where it is**. It can be **physical**, **chemical** or **biological**.

**Freeze–thaw** (physical weathering): rainwater gets into a crack, **freezes and expands**, and pushes the crack wider. The ice melts, more water gets in, and it happens again and again until bits break off. Hot days and cold nights can crack rock too.
**Chemical weathering:** rain is slightly **acidic**. It **reacts** with rocks like **limestone, chalk and marble** and slowly dissolves them.
**Biological weathering:** **plant roots** grow into cracks and force them apart; burrowing animals break rock up too.
**Erosion** is the **movement** (transport) of the broken bits by **water, wind, ice** or gravity. As they are carried they bash together and become **smaller and rounder**.
**Deposition:** where the water slows down (a lake or the sea), the bits settle in layers of **sediment**. Over time they are **compacted** and **cemented** into **sedimentary rock**.

**The rock cycle:** heat and pressure turn rock into **metamorphic** rock; **melting** makes **magma**; **cooling** turns magma into **igneous** rock; **weathering and erosion** start it all again. The cycle takes **millions of years**.
Some changes are **fast**: a volcanic eruption, earthquake, landslide or flood can change the land in hours. Others are **very slow**: sediment builds up only millimetres a year.

Many rock-cycle changes are **physical changes** like everyday ones — melting and setting (like candle wax), mud settling out of water. **Chemical weathering** is different: it is a **chemical reaction** that makes new substances.

facts: The **Sun** is a **star** at the centre of our **Solar System**. Its **gravity** keeps eight **planets** in **orbit** around it.
In order from the Sun: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. A way to remember: **M**y **V**ery **E**asy **M**ethod **J**ust **S**peeds **U**p **N**aming.
The four **inner planets** are small and **rocky**. The four **outer planets** are **giants** made mostly of gas and ice. Pluto is now called a **dwarf planet**.
An **orbit** is the path an object takes around a larger one. Earth takes **one year** to orbit the Sun; planets further out take **longer**.
A **moon** is a **natural satellite** — it orbits a planet. Our Moon orbits the Earth about once a month.
Only stars give out their own light. We see **planets and moons** because they **reflect sunlight**.

The Sun always lights **half** of the Moon. As the Moon orbits, we see **different amounts of the lit half**: **new moon → crescent → first quarter → gibbous → full moon → gibbous → last quarter → crescent → new moon**, about every 29½ days.

Long ago most people thought the **Earth was at the centre** and everything moved round it (the **geocentric** model). In the 1500s **Copernicus** put the **Sun at the centre** (the **heliocentric** model); **Galileo**'s telescope then showed moons orbiting Jupiter, which backed him up.

topics.title: Day, night, years and seasons
topics.summary: How the spinning, tilted Earth orbiting the Sun gives us day and night, years, seasons and changing day length.

images.caption: The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day; the other half has night.
The tilted Earth in June and December. The axis always points the same way, so in June the UK leans towards the Sun.
images.title: The seasons

facts: The Earth **spins on its axis** once every **24 hours**. The half facing the Sun has **day**; the half facing away has **night**.
The Earth spins from **west to east**, so the Sun appears to **rise in the east** and **set in the west**. The Sun isn't moving across the sky — we are turning.
The Earth **orbits the Sun** once a **year** — 365¼ days. The extra quarters add up to a **leap day** every 4 years.

The Earth's axis is **tilted** (about 23½°) and always points the same way in space. The **tilt** causes the **seasons** — **not** how close we are to the Sun (the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January).

**UK summer (June):** the northern hemisphere tilts **towards** the Sun. The Sun is **higher** in the sky, the **days are longer**, and the sunlight is **more concentrated** (less spread out), so it is warmer.
**UK winter (December):** the northern hemisphere tilts **away** from the Sun. The Sun stays **low**, the **days are short**, and the same sunlight is **spread over a bigger area**, so it is colder.
The **southern hemisphere** has the **opposite** seasons: when it is summer in the UK, it is winter in Australia.
Day length hardly changes at the **equator** (about 12 hours all year). Near the **poles** it changes the most: **24 hours of daylight** in summer and **24 hours of darkness** in winter.
The higher the Sun, the **shorter the shadows**: midday shadows are shortest in summer and longest in winter.

questions.stem: Explain why the UK has longer days and warmer weather in summer than in winter.

acceptablePoints.point: the Earth's axis is tilted
in summer the northern hemisphere / UK is tilted towards the Sun (in winter, away from it)
so the UK spends more of each 24-hour spin in sunlight / longer days

award.4: any four points

markScheme.modelAnswer: The Earth's axis is tilted. In summer the northern hemisphere, where the UK is, is tilted towards the Sun, so the UK spends more of each 24 hours in sunlight and the days are longer. The Sun is also higher in the sky, so its light is more concentrated on each area of ground and heats it more. In winter the UK is tilted away, so the days are short and the light is spread out.

topics.title: Stars, galaxies and light years
topics.summary: How huge the Universe is: stars, exoplanets and galaxies, the light year, and why the scale matters for exploring space.

table.title: How long light takes to reach us
head: From
Light takes about
rows: the nearest star after the Sun (Proxima Centauri)
the most distant galaxies we can see

facts: A **star** is a huge ball of very hot gas that **gives out its own light**. The Sun is our nearest star. Many stars have planets orbiting them.
An **exoplanet** is a planet that orbits a star **other than the Sun**. Astronomers have found thousands.
A **galaxy** is an enormous collection of **billions of stars** held together by **gravity**. Ours is the **Milky Way**; the whole Solar System is a tiny part of it.
The **Universe** contains **billions of galaxies**. From smallest to biggest: **planet → solar system → galaxy → Universe**.

Light is the fastest thing there is — about **300 000 km every second**. Even so, sunlight takes about **8 minutes** to reach us, light from the nearest other star about **4 years**, and light from other galaxies **millions or billions of years**.
A **light year** is a **distance**, not a time: how far light travels in one year — over **9 million million km** (about 9.5 million million km).

Choose a **unit that fits the distance**: **kilometres** on Earth; **astronomical units** (1 AU = the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km) in the Solar System; **light years** for stars and galaxies, so the numbers stay sensible.
Because light takes time to travel, we see distant stars and galaxies **as they were in the past**.

Space is so big that people have only travelled as far as the **Moon**. Robot **probes** take years to reach the outer planets and would take tens of thousands of years to reach the nearest star — so we learn about stars by studying their **light** with **telescopes**.

topics.title: The skeleton
topics.summary: The names of the main bones and the five jobs the skeleton does.

images.caption: The main bones of the human skeleton. An adult has 206 bones.

facts: The skeleton has **five jobs**: **support** (holds the body up), **protection** (skull protects the brain, ribs protect the heart and lungs), **movement** (muscles pull on bones), **making blood cells** (in the bone marrow) and **storing minerals** such as calcium.
**Skull** — protects the brain. **Vertebrae** (backbone / spine) — protect the spinal cord. **Ribs** — protect the heart and lungs.
Arm: **humerus** (upper arm), **radius** and **ulna** (forearm — the ulna is on the little-finger side).
Leg: **femur** (thigh — the longest and strongest bone), **patella** (kneecap), **tibia** (shin) and **fibula** (the thinner bone beside the tibia).
Shoulder and chest: **clavicle** (collarbone), **scapula** (shoulder blade), **sternum** (breastbone). Hip: **pelvis**.
An adult has **206 bones**. Bones are living tissue: they grow, repair and contain blood vessels and nerves.

Use the exam words for the jobs: **support**, **protection**, **movement** and **making blood cells** (in the bone marrow). “Keeps us together” or “holds us up” won't get the mark — write **support**.

A bird's **wing** and your **arm** have the **same bones** (humerus, radius, ulna) but **different jobs**: the wing is for **flying** (flapping pushes air down and lifts the bird), the arm and hand are for **lifting, carrying, holding and gripping** things.

topics.title: Movement at joints
topics.summary: Where bones meet: the types of joint, and the tissues that hold them together and keep them moving smoothly.

images.caption: The main types of joint and where you find them.

facts: A **joint** is where two or more bones meet. Without joints the skeleton couldn't bend.
**Hinge joint** — moves in one direction, like a door hinge: the **knee** and the **elbow**.
**Ball-and-socket joint** — moves in all directions: the **hip** and the **shoulder**.
**Pivot joint** — lets one bone turn on another: the **neck** (turning your head). **Fixed joints** don't move at all: the plates of the **skull**.
**Ligaments** are tough, slightly stretchy bands that join **bone to bone** and hold the joint together.
**Cartilage** is a smooth, rubbery layer on the ends of bones that stops them rubbing and absorbs shocks. **Synovial fluid** oils the joint so it moves smoothly.
**Tendons** join **muscle to bone** — that's how a muscle pulls on a bone to move it (more in the next topic).

topics.title: Muscles and antagonistic pairs
topics.summary: How muscles move bones by pulling, why they come in pairs, and the names and places of the main muscles.

images.caption: The biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair. When one contracts, the other relaxes.
The main muscles of the body.
The leg from the revision sheet: D quadriceps, A hamstrings, C tibialis anterior, B gastrocnemius (with the soleus underneath).

facts: Muscles move bones by **contracting** (getting shorter and pulling). Muscles can only **pull — they can never push**.
Because they can't push, muscles work in **antagonistic pairs**: one contracts while the other **relaxes**. They pull the bone in opposite directions.
To **bend** (flex) the arm, the **biceps contracts** and the triceps relaxes. To **straighten** (extend) it, the **triceps contracts** and the biceps relaxes.

Other antagonistic pairs: **quadriceps** (front of thigh) and **hamstrings** (back of thigh) at the knee; **tibialis anterior** (front of shin) and **gastrocnemius** (calf) at the ankle; **abdominals** and back muscles.
Muscles are attached to bones by **tendons**.

Names to know: **deltoids** (shoulders), **pectorals** (chest), **biceps/triceps** (upper arm), **abdominals** (stomach), **trapezius** (upper back/neck), **latissimus dorsi** (back), **gluteals** (bottom), **quadriceps** and **hamstrings** (thigh), **tibialis anterior** (front of shin), **gastrocnemius** and **soleus** (calf).

The calf has two muscles: the **gastrocnemius** on the outside and the **soleus** underneath it. Both join the **Achilles tendon** and point the toes. The **tibialis anterior** on the front of the shin does the opposite: it lifts the toes.
**Use the scientific names** in tests: gastrocnemius, not "calf muscle"; tibia, not "shin bone". The everyday name in brackets is only there to help you remember.

topics.title: Levels of organisation
topics.summary: How living things are built up: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism — and what the main organ systems and plant organs do.

images.caption: From one cell to a whole organism. Each level is made of the one before it.

facts: A **cell** is the smallest building block of a living thing. Every living thing is made of cells.
A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together — muscle tissue, nerve tissue, the lining of your stomach.
An **organ** is made of different tissues working together to do a job — the heart, the stomach, a leaf.
An **organ system** is a group of organs working together — the digestive system (mouth, stomach, intestines), the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels).
An **organism** is a complete living thing, made of organ systems working together — you, a cat, an oak tree.
The order, smallest first: **cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism**. A trick: Cats Taste Of Old Socks.
**Digestive system** (mouth, stomach, intestines) — breaks food down into small molecules and **absorbs** them into the blood.
**Circulatory system** (heart, blood vessels, blood) — **transports** substances such as oxygen and food molecules **around the body**.
**Respiratory system** — also called the **gas exchange system** (lungs, windpipe) — takes **oxygen** into the blood and removes **carbon dioxide**.
**Reproductive system** — produces **sex cells** (sperm in males, eggs in females) so that new humans can be made.
**Skeletal** and **muscular systems** work together for support and movement; the **nervous system** (brain, spinal cord, nerves) carries messages.

Plants have organs too: the **root** anchors the plant in the soil and absorbs **water** (and minerals); the **stem** holds the plant **upright** and carries water up; the **leaf** absorbs **sunlight** to make food by **photosynthesis**; the **flower** is for reproduction.

topics.title: The microscope
topics.summary: The parts of a light microscope, how to use it, and how to work out magnification.

images.caption: The parts of a light microscope.

facts: **Eyepiece lens** — the lens you look through (usually ×10). **Objective lenses** — the lenses just above the specimen, on a turning **nosepiece** (usually ×4, ×10, ×40).
**Stage** — the flat platform the slide sits on, held by **stage clips**. **Light** (lamp or mirror) under the stage shines through the specimen.
**Coarse focusing wheel** — big movements to get the image roughly sharp. **Fine focusing wheel** — small movements to make it clear.
**Arm** — carry the microscope by this (and support the **base**). The **tube** holds the eyepiece.

To use it: put the slide on the stage, start with the **lowest-power objective**, turn the **coarse** wheel until you see the image, then the **fine** wheel to sharpen it. Then switch to a higher power.
**Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.** Eyepiece ×10 with objective ×40 = ×400.
**Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.** A cell 0.1 mm wide that appears 40 mm wide is magnified ×400.
**Why a microscope?** Cells are **too small to see with the naked eye**. A microscope **magnifies** them (makes them look bigger) so you can see their parts.

**Preparing a slide:** the sample must be **very thin** (one layer of cells) so that **light can pass through it**. A **stain** is added to make cells and their parts (like the nucleus) **easier to see** — **iodine** for plant cells such as onion, **methylene blue** for cheek cells. A **cover slip** keeps the sample flat and stops it drying out.

**Using it step by step:** (1) put the slide on the stage and hold it with the clips; (2) choose the **lowest-power objective**; (3) **looking from the side**, turn the coarse wheel so the lens comes close to the slide without touching it; (4) look through the eyepiece and turn the **coarse wheel** the other way until the cells appear; (5) sharpen with the **fine wheel**; (6) turn to a **higher-power objective** (×10, ×20, ×40) and refocus with the **fine wheel** only.

topics.title: Plant and animal cells
topics.summary: The parts of a cell, what each one does, and the three extra parts only plant cells have.

images.caption: An animal cell and a plant cell. The plant cell has three extra parts.

facts: **Both** animal and plant cells have a **nucleus**, **cytoplasm**, a **cell membrane** and **mitochondria**.
**Nucleus** — controls the cell and contains the **genetic information** (DNA / chromosomes).
**Cytoplasm** — the jelly where the cell's **chemical reactions** happen.
**Cell membrane** — a thin skin that **controls what goes in and out** of the cell.
**Mitochondria** — where **respiration** happens, **releasing energy** from food (glucose).

**Only plant cells** have a **cell wall** (made of cellulose — gives support and shape), **chloroplasts** (contain green **chlorophyll** for **photosynthesis**) and a **permanent vacuole** (full of cell sap — keeps the cell firm).
Plant cells have a regular, box-like shape because of the cell wall. Animal cells are irregular and can change shape.

topics.title: Specialised cells
topics.summary: Cells with a special shape or extra parts to do one job well: nerve, sperm, leaf (palisade), root hair and red blood cells.

images.caption: Five specialised cells and the adaptations that suit them to their job.

facts: A **specialised cell** has a shape or special features (**adaptations**) that suit it to one particular job.
**Nerve cell** — very **long**, with **branched ends** to connect to other cells. Job: carries **electrical signals** (impulses) quickly around the body.
**Sperm cell** — a **tail** to swim to the egg, lots of **mitochondria** for energy, and a head with **enzymes** to get into the egg. Carries **half** the genetic information.
**Leaf (palisade) cell** — packed with **chloroplasts** for **photosynthesis**; tall and thin so lots fit at the top of the leaf where the light is.
**Root hair cell** — a **long, thin extension** that gives a **large surface area** to **absorb water and minerals** from the soil. No chloroplasts — it's underground, in the dark.
**Red blood cell** — a **biconcave disc** (dented both sides) for a big surface area, **no nucleus** so there is more room for **haemoglobin**, which carries **oxygen**.

topics.title: Unicellular organisms
topics.summary: Living things made of just one cell: amoeba, euglena, bacteria and yeast.

images.caption: Four unicellular organisms. Each single cell does everything the organism needs.

facts: A **unicellular** organism is made of **one cell only**. That single cell does everything — feeding, moving, getting rid of waste, reproducing. **Multicellular** organisms (like us) are made of many cells.
**Amoeba** — lives in pond water. It moves and feeds by pushing out **pseudopodia** ('false feet') and wrapping around its food. A **contractile vacuole** squeezes out extra water.
**Euglena** — also in ponds. Has **chloroplasts** so it can photosynthesise like a plant, but swims with a **flagellum** (a whip-like tail) like an animal. An **eyespot** senses light.

**Bacteria** — very small, with **no nucleus**: the DNA floats in a loop in the cytoplasm. They have a cell wall (not cellulose), and some have a **flagellum** to move. They reproduce by splitting in two.
**Yeast** — a single-celled **fungus**. It has a nucleus and a cell wall, and reproduces by **budding**. Used to make bread rise and to brew beer (it makes carbon dioxide).
Unicellular organisms are so small you need a **microscope** to see them.
