topics.title: Diffusion
topics.summary: How particles spread out from where there are lots of them to where there are few — and why that matters for cells.

images.caption: Particles spread out from a high concentration to a low concentration until they are evenly mixed.

facts: **Diffusion** is the **net movement of particles** from an area of **high concentration** to an area of **low concentration** — from where there are lots to where there are few.
It happens because particles in liquids and gases are always **moving randomly**. Over time they spread out until they are **evenly mixed**.
Diffusion is **passive** — it needs **no energy** from the cell.
The difference in concentration is the **concentration gradient**. A **bigger** difference means **faster** diffusion.
Diffusion is also faster when it's **warmer** (particles move faster), over a **shorter distance**, and with a **larger surface area**.
Examples: **oxygen** diffuses from the lungs into the blood; **carbon dioxide** diffuses out of the blood into the lungs; glucose diffuses from the gut into the blood; a smell spreads across a room.
Cells get what they need (oxygen, glucose) and get rid of waste (carbon dioxide) by diffusion across the **cell membrane**.

topics.title: Food chains and food webs
topics.summary: Who eats whom: producers, consumers, and how food chains join up into a food web.

images.caption: A woodland food web. Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.

facts: An **ecosystem** is all the living things in an area together with their non-living **environment** — the air, water and soil around them.
A **population** is all the organisms of **one species** living in an area, such as all the rabbits in a field.
**Producers** are green plants and algae. They make their own food by photosynthesis, using light energy from the **Sun**. Every food chain starts with a producer.
**Consumers** are animals: they get their energy by eating other living things. **Herbivores** eat plants, **carnivores** eat animals and **omnivores** eat both.
A **food chain** shows what eats what. The **arrows point from the food to the animal that eats it** — the direction the energy flows.
In grass → rabbit → fox, the rabbit is the **primary consumer** and the fox the **secondary consumer**. The animal at the end of a chain, which nothing else eats, is the **top predator**.
A **predator** hunts and eats other animals; the animals it eats are its **prey**.
A **food web** is several food chains joined together. Most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator.
To **combine food chains** into a web, write each organism only once, then draw every arrow from every chain.

topics.title: Changing populations
topics.summary: Why the number of one organism rises or falls, and how that change spreads through a food web.

images.caption: Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in turn. The foxes' peaks come after the rabbits' peaks.

facts: Organisms in a food web **depend on each other** for food and nutrients — this is **interdependence**. A change in one population changes others.
The size of a population depends on the number of **predators**, the amount of **food (prey)**, **disease**, **pollution** and **competition**.

**Competition**: there is not enough of everything for everyone. Animals compete for **food, water, space and mates**; plants compete for **light, water, space and minerals (nutrients)** from the soil.

**Predator and prey cycle**: lots of prey → more food, so more predators survive and breed → more prey are eaten and prey numbers fall → predators go hungry and fall → prey recover. The predator peaks come **after** the prey peaks.
If one population falls, look **both ways** in the web: its predators may fall (less food) and its food may rise (less is eaten). Other prey may be eaten more instead.
**Environmental changes** — a cold winter, a drought, a flood, a hedge or wood cut down — change the food, water and shelter available, so populations change.
**Toxic materials** such as pesticides or oil spills can kill organisms directly, or kill their food.

A **new species brought into an area** can upset a food web: it may eat the native species, compete with them, spread disease, and often has no predators of its own. Grey squirrels from North America have pushed out red squirrels across most of England.
With population **data**, look at what changed just **before** the rise or fall — a new predator, a hard winter, a disease — to work out the most likely cause.

topics.title: Decomposers, toxins and pollinators
topics.summary: How decomposers recycle nutrients, why poisons build up along food chains, and why we need pollinating insects.
facts: **Decomposers** — mostly **bacteria** and **fungi** — break down dead plants, dead animals and animal waste.
This **recycles nutrients** (minerals) back into the soil or water. Plants take them up through their roots and use them to grow — so the nutrients go round again.
Without decomposers, dead material would pile up and plants would run out of nutrients. Every level of a food web depends on them.
**Toxic materials** such as some **pesticides** or **mercury** can get into food chains. Some cannot be broken down or got rid of, so they **build up** in an animal's body.
Each animal eats **many** of the organisms below it, so the toxin gets **more concentrated at each step**. The **top predator** gets the biggest dose and may die or fail to breed.
In the 1950s–60s, the pesticide **DDT** built up in birds of prey such as peregrine falcons; their eggshells became so thin that numbers crashed. DDT is now banned in the UK.
Humans are at the top of many food chains, so toxins can end up in **our food** — large fish such as tuna can contain more mercury than small fish.

**Insects are needed to pollinate many food crops** — apples, strawberries, beans, oilseed rape. Without pollination, the fruits and seeds do not form. (Wheat, rice and maize are pollinated by the wind.)
**Bee numbers are falling** because of pesticides, disease and parasites, and the loss of wild flowers and hedgerows. Fewer pollinators means smaller harvests, dearer food and less choice.

markScheme.modelAnswer: Bees are pollinators: they carry pollen from flower to flower. Many food crops, such as apples, strawberries and beans, need insects to pollinate them. topics.summary: The male and female parts of a flower, and what each part does.

table.title: The parts of a flower and their jobs
head: Part

facts: **Flowers** hold a plant's **reproductive organs**. Many flowers have both male and female parts.
The **stamen** is the **male** part. It is made of the **anther**, which makes **pollen**, and the **filament**, the stalk that holds the anther up.
**Pollen** grains contain the plant's **male sex cells**.
The **carpel** is the **female** part. It is made of the **stigma** (the sticky top where pollen lands), the **style** (the stalk) and the **ovary**.
Inside the ovary are the **ovules**. Each one contains a **female sex cell**, and after fertilisation it becomes a **seed**.
**Petals** are often brightly coloured and scented to **attract insects**. **Nectaries** at the base make sugary **nectar** as a reward.
**Sepals** are small, green, leaf-like parts under the petals. They **protect the flower while it is a bud**.
Watch the spelling: the **ovary** holds the **ovules** — the ovary becomes the fruit, each ovule becomes a seed.
keywords: sticky top of the carpel where pollen lands

topics.title: Pollination and fertilisation
topics.summary: How pollen gets from flower to flower, how the sex cells join, and how seeds and fruits form.

images.caption: After pollination a pollen tube grows down to an ovule.

table.title: Wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers
head: Feature
Wind-pollinated
Insect-pollinated
rows: hang outside the flower on long filaments
inside the flower, where insects brush past
large and feathery, hanging outside to catch pollen
huge amounts; small, light and smooth

facts: Flowering plants reproduce **sexually**: a male sex cell (from pollen) joins with a female sex cell (in an ovule).
**Pollination** is the **transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma**, on the same plant or another plant of the same kind.
Pollen is carried by the **wind**, by **insects**, or by other animals such as birds and bats.

**Fertilisation** comes after pollination: a **pollen tube** grows from the pollen grain down through the **style** to an ovule. The **male nucleus** moves down the tube and **joins the nucleus** of the female sex cell.
After fertilisation the **ovule becomes a seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**. The petals and stamens wither and drop off.
A **seed** contains the **embryo** (the tiny new plant) and a **food store**, inside a tough coat. A **fruit** is the ripened ovary with the seeds inside.

**Wind-pollinated** flowers are small and dull, with no scent or nectar; their anthers and feathery stigmas hang out in the wind, and they make **huge amounts** of light pollen because most of it is wasted.
**Insect-pollinated** flowers have bright petals, scent and nectar; the pollen is sticky or spiky so it clings to insects.

**Plant breeders** use pollination for **selective breeding**: they remove a flower's anthers, brush on pollen from a plant with a feature they want, then cover the flower with a bag so no other pollen gets in.

topics.title: Seed dispersal
topics.summary: How plants spread their seeds by wind, water and animals, and why it matters.

images.caption: Five ways seeds get away from the parent plant.

table.title: Ways of dispersing seeds
head: Method
Features of the fruit or seed
Examples
rows: light; wings that spin, or a parachute of hairs
light, waterproof, with air inside so it floats
juicy, brightly coloured fruit; seeds with tough coats come out in droppings
hooks that catch on fur or clothes

facts: **Seed dispersal** means spreading seeds **away from the parent plant**.
Seeds that drop right under the parent would **compete** with it and with each other for **light, water, space and minerals**, and be shaded by its leaves. Spread out, more seedlings survive.
Dispersal also lets a species **reach new places**, so it survives even if one area is cleared, flooded or crowded.
**Wind**: light fruits with **wings** (sycamore spins and falls slowly) or a **parachute of hairs** (dandelion) are carried far by the wind.
**Water**: fruits that are light, waterproof and full of air **float** — a coconut can drift across an ocean.

**Animals**: **juicy, brightly coloured** fruits are eaten; the seeds have tough coats, pass through the gut unharmed and come out in **droppings**, far away. Fruits with **hooks** catch on fur and drop off later.
Some pods dry out and **burst open**, flinging the seeds away (peas, gorse).
To **work out** how a seed is dispersed, look at its features: wings or hairs → wind; floats → water; juicy and colourful → eaten; hooks → stuck on fur.
Plants make **many** seeds because most land where they cannot grow or are eaten — making lots means some will survive.

the plant that made the seeds

questions.stem: Name one plant whose seeds are dispersed by the wind.

questions.stem: Why does a dandelion make hundreds of seeds?

questions.stem: How does a dandelion's parachute of hairs make it more likely to produce offspring that survive?

questions.stem: Explain why seed dispersal is important for the survival of the parent plant and its offspring.

acceptablePoints.point: seeds that fall near the parent would compete with it for light, water, space and minerals
the parent's leaves would shade the seedlings, so they get less light for photosynthesis
the seedlings would also compete with each other, so fewer would survive
spreading the seeds out means less competition, so more seedlings survive and the parent is not weakened
seeds can reach new areas, so the species survives even if one place becomes unsuitable

award.3: one mark for each point, up to 3

markScheme.modelAnswer: If the seeds fell under the parent plant, the seedlings would compete with the parent and with each other for light, water, space and minerals, and the parent's leaves would shade them. Dispersal spreads the seeds away, so there is less competition: more seedlings survive and the parent is not weakened. It also lets the plant reach new areas, so the species survives even if one place changes.

topics.title: Variation and species
topics.summary: Why living things differ, and whether a difference comes from genes, the environment or both.
facts: A **species** is a group of living things that have more in common with each other than with any other group. Members of a species can breed together.
**Variation** means the differences between living things. There is variation **between species** (a zebra and a horse) and **within a species** (two people).
**Inherited variation** comes from the **genes** passed on by your parents — for example blood group and natural eye colour.
**Environmental variation** comes from your surroundings and the way you live — for example a scar, the language you speak or dyed hair.
Many characteristics are affected by **both** genes and the environment. Your genes set a possible height, but **diet** and health affect how tall you actually grow.
**Identical twins** have the same genes, so any differences between them are caused by the **environment**.
To decide what causes a characteristic, ask: could it be changed by the way you live? If not, it is probably inherited; if it is also passed on in families, it is probably both.
keywords: a group of living things with more in common with each other than with other groups
the differences within and between species
a feature of a living thing, such as eye colour
passed on from parents in genes
instructions passed from parents that control many characteristics
twins with exactly the same genes

markScheme.modelAnswer: The student is not right. Height is partly inherited, because genes from your parents affect how tall you can grow. But the environment matters too: a poor diet or illness while growing can stop someone reaching that height. Identical twins can end up different heights, which shows it is not only genes.

topics.title: Continuous and discontinuous variation
topics.summary: Two kinds of variation, and which graph to draw for each.

images.caption: Blood group (discontinuous) as a bar chart with gaps; height (continuous) as a histogram with a line through it.

table.title: The two kinds of variation
head: Continuous
Discontinuous
rows: height, body mass, arm span, foot length, leaf length
blood group, eye colour, tongue rolling, earlobes free or attached
histogram or line graph — bars touch

facts: **Continuous variation:** the characteristic can have **any value** within a range — you measure it. Height, body mass and hand span are examples.
**Discontinuous variation:** the characteristic can only be sorted into **categories** — you count how many are in each. Blood group (A, B, AB, O) and whether you can roll your tongue are examples.
Show **discontinuous** data in a **bar chart**: one bar per category, with **gaps** between the bars.
Show **continuous** data in a **histogram** (bars touching) or a **line graph**. First group the measurements into equal ranges, such as 140–144 cm, 145–149 cm.
On both graphs the **y-axis** shows the **number of people** (or plants, animals) in each group.
A graph of continuous variation, such as height, usually makes a **hump shape**: most people are near the middle and few are very short or very tall.
Continuous characteristics are usually affected by **genes and the environment**; discontinuous ones are usually controlled by **genes only**.

differences that can only be grouped into categories
a group, such as blood group A
graph with separate bars and gaps, for categories

topics.title: Variation, adaptation and survival
topics.summary: How adaptations and variation help a species survive in a changing environment.
facts: An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an organism **survive** in its environment. Adaptations are **inherited** — an animal cannot choose to grow one.

Examples: a **polar bear** has thick fur and a layer of fat to keep warm; an **arctic hare** has white fur for **camouflage** in the snow; a **camel** has wide feet that do not sink into sand and stores fat in its hump; a **cactus** has spines instead of leaves to lose less water and stop animals eating it.
Environments are **always changing**: the climate warms or cools, a new **disease** or **predator** arrives, or food runs short.
Because of **variation**, some individuals in a species have features that suit the new conditions better. They are **more likely to survive and reproduce**.
Their young **inherit** those helpful features, so over many generations the features become **more common**.
A species with **lots of variation** is more likely to survive a change. A species with **very little variation** could be wiped out — it may become **extinct**.
**Extinct** means every member of the species has died out, so it can never come back.

questions.stem: Explain how variation within a species can help it survive when its environment changes.

acceptablePoints.point: individuals in a species are different / show variation
some individuals have characteristics that are better suited to the new conditions
these individuals are more likely to survive
they reproduce and pass on their (inherited) characteristics to their young

markScheme.modelAnswer: Members of a species are not all the same. When the environment changes, for example it gets colder, some individuals have features that suit the new conditions, such as thicker fur. They are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those features on to their young. So the species carries on instead of becoming extinct — a species with no variation might all die.

topics.title: The reproductive systems
topics.summary: The organs of the female and male reproductive systems and what each one does.

images.caption: The female reproductive system (front view).
The male reproductive system (front view).

facts: The **reproductive system** is all the organs involved in reproduction.
**Ovaries** contain the eggs. About once a month, one egg is released.
The **oviduct** (fallopian tube) carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus. **Fertilisation happens in the oviduct.**
The **uterus** (womb) is where a baby develops. Its **lining** builds up each month, ready for a fertilised egg.
The **cervix** is a ring of muscle at the entrance to the uterus; it holds the baby in during pregnancy. The **vagina** is where sperm are received and the baby leaves the body at birth.
The **testes** (one: testis) make sperm. They hang outside the body in the **scrotum**, where it is a little cooler — best for making sperm.
The **sperm duct** carries sperm from a testis to the urethra. **Glands** add a fluid that gives sperm nutrients; sperm plus fluid is **semen**.
The **urethra** carries semen (or urine — never both at once) through the **penis**, which carries sperm out of the male's body.

topics.title: Sex cells, the menstrual cycle and fertility
topics.summary: Sperm and egg cells, the 28-day menstrual cycle, and what can make it hard to have a baby.

images.caption: A sperm cell and an egg cell (not to scale).
What happens in the uterus during one menstrual cycle.

facts: A **gamete** is a sex cell. The male gamete is the **sperm**; the female gamete is the **egg** (ovum).
**Sperm** are adapted to swim to the egg: a **tail** to swim, lots of **mitochondria** to release energy, and a **head** holding the nucleus.
The **egg** is much bigger: its **cytoplasm** is a food store for the early embryo, and its **jelly coat** changes after fertilisation so only one sperm gets in.
The **menstrual cycle** lasts about **28 days**. It prepares the female body for pregnancy.
**Days 1–5: menstruation** (a period) — the lining of the uterus breaks down and leaves through the vagina. **Days 5–14:** the lining **builds up** again.
**About day 14: ovulation** — an egg is released from an ovary and moves along the oviduct. The lining **stays thick**, ready for a fertilised egg.
If the egg is **not fertilised**, the lining breaks down and the cycle starts again. If it **is fertilised**, it settles into the lining and the periods **stop** during pregnancy.
Pregnancy is **most likely around ovulation**, when an egg is in the oviduct (sperm can survive a few days).

**Low fertility** — in males: a **low sperm count**, sperm that **cannot swim well**, or blocked sperm ducts. In females: **not releasing eggs**, or **blocked oviducts** so egg and sperm cannot meet. Age, smoking and heavy drinking can also lower fertility. Fertility treatments can help, for example drugs that make the ovaries release eggs, or **IVF**, where eggs are fertilised outside the body.

choices: the egg grows into an embryo anyway
the lining stays thick for the rest of the year
questions.explain: Without a fertilised egg, the lining is not needed, so it breaks down and the cycle starts again.

questions.stem: When in the menstrual cycle is a woman most likely to become pregnant?
questions.answer: around the middle of the cycle, close to ovulation
choices: equally on every day of the cycle
questions.explain: An egg is only available for a short time after ovulation, so that is when fertilisation is most likely.

questions.stem: Which of these can cause low fertility in a woman?
questions.answer: blocked oviducts, so the egg and sperm cannot meet
choices: a thick uterus lining before ovulation
questions.explain: If the oviducts are blocked, sperm cannot reach the egg.

questions.stem: Which of these can cause low fertility in a man?
choices: sperm with long tails that swim well
questions.explain: With few sperm, it is less likely that one will reach the egg.

topics.title: Fertilisation, pregnancy and birth
topics.summary: How a fertilised egg grows into a baby, how the placenta looks after it, and what happens at birth.

images.caption: From sex cells to birth.
A foetus in the uterus near the end of pregnancy.

table.title: What crosses the placenta?
head: From mother to foetus
From foetus to mother
Harmful things that can also cross

facts: **Fertilisation** is when the nucleus of a sperm joins with the nucleus of an egg. It happens in the **oviduct**.
The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells, the **embryo**. It moves to the uterus and **settles into the lining** (implantation).
**Gestation** is the time the baby develops in the uterus: about **9 months** (around 40 weeks) in humans. The developing baby is called a **foetus** once its organs have started to form.

The **placenta** is an organ attached to the uterus wall. It passes **oxygen and nutrients** from the mother's blood to the foetus, and takes **waste** such as carbon dioxide back. The two bloods **do not mix**.
The **umbilical cord** connects the foetus to the placenta. **Amniotic fluid** surrounds the foetus and **cushions** it from bumps.

**Harmful substances** can also cross the placenta: **alcohol**, **nicotine** and **carbon monoxide** from cigarettes, some drugs and some viruses. This is why pregnant women are advised not to smoke or drink alcohol.
**Birth:** the **cervix widens**, the **muscles of the uterus contract** and push the baby out through the **vagina**. The cord is cut, and the placenta comes out afterwards.

a ball of cells growing from a fertilised egg
the time a baby develops in the uterus
organ that gives the foetus oxygen and nutrients and removes waste
connects the foetus to the placenta
liquid that surrounds and protects the foetus
muscles tightening, as the uterus does during birth

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is advised not to smoke or drink alcohol. Explain why, using what you know about the placenta.

acceptablePoints.point: the foetus gets substances from the mother's blood through the placenta (and umbilical cord)
useful substances such as oxygen and nutrients pass across the placenta to the foetus
harmful substances such as alcohol, nicotine or carbon monoxide can also cross the placenta into the foetus

this can harm the foetus: slower growth / low birth weight / born early / damage to developing organs or brain

award.4: any four of the points, one mark each

markScheme.modelAnswer: The foetus gets everything it needs from the mother's blood through the placenta, such as oxygen and nutrients. But harmful substances can cross the placenta too. Alcohol can damage the developing organs and brain. Smoking puts nicotine and carbon monoxide into the blood; carbon monoxide means less oxygen reaches the foetus, so it may grow more slowly and be born small or early.

questions.stem: Describe the stages from the production of sex cells to the birth of a baby.

acceptablePoints.point: sperm are made in the testes and eggs are in the ovaries
an egg is released from an ovary (ovulation) and moves along the oviduct
sperm are released into the vagina and swim through the cervix and uterus to the oviduct
fertilisation happens in the oviduct: the nucleus of a sperm joins with the nucleus of the egg
the fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells (an embryo), which settles into the lining of the uterus
the embryo grows into a foetus over about 9 months (gestation), getting oxygen and nutrients from the placenta through the umbilical cord, protected by amniotic fluid
at birth the cervix widens and the muscles of the uterus contract, pushing the baby out through the vagina

award.6: six of the points, in a sensible order
award.4: four points in a sensible order

markScheme.modelAnswer: Sperm are made in the testes, and eggs are stored in the ovaries. About once a month an egg is released (ovulation) and moves along the oviduct. Sperm released into the vagina swim through the cervix and uterus into the oviduct, where one sperm's nucleus joins with the egg's nucleus — fertilisation. The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells, the embryo, which settles into the uterus lining. Over about nine months it grows into a foetus, fed with oxygen and nutrients through the placenta and umbilical cord and cushioned by amniotic fluid. At birth the cervix widens and the uterus muscles contract to push the baby out through the vagina.

questions.tip: Go in order: sex cells → fertilisation → embryo → foetus → birth.

topics.title: Types of enquiry
topics.summary: The different ways scientists answer questions — and how to tell which one a question needs.

table.title: Types of enquiry
head: Type
What you do
Example question
rows: change one variable, keep the others the same, measure what happens
Does the temperature of water change how fast sugar dissolves?
look closely, sometimes over time or with a microscope, and record what you see
What parts of a cell can I see under a light microscope?
collect lots of data where you can't control everything, and look for a link
Do people with longer legs jump further?
sort things into groups by their features, often with a key
Which group does this animal belong to?
find out from books, websites or experts
What did Robert Hooke see with his microscope?

facts: A **fair test** changes **one** thing and keeps everything else the same, so you know what caused the result.
The variable you **change** is the **independent variable**; the one you **measure** is the **dependent variable**; the ones you keep the same are **control variables**.
An **observation** enquiry means looking carefully and recording what you see — for example cells under a microscope, or a plant growing over a week.
**Pattern seeking** looks for a link in lots of data when you can't control the other variables — for example surveys of people.
Clue words: “Does … affect …?” → fair test. “What can I see …?” → observation. “Do people/things that … also …?” → pattern seeking.
keywords: change one variable, keep the rest the same
look for a link in lots of data

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “What parts of an onion cell can I see under a microscope?”
questions.explain: You look and record what you see — observation.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “Does the temperature of water affect how fast salt dissolves?”
questions.explain: Change one thing (temperature), keep the rest the same, measure — a fair test.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this question: “Do people with bigger hands have bigger feet?”
questions.explain: You can't change people's hands — you collect lots of data and look for a link.

questions.stem: What type of enquiry is this: sorting leaves into groups with a key?
questions.explain: Sorting into groups by features is identifying and classifying.

questions.stem: In a fair test, what do you call the variable you change?
questions.explain: Independent = the one you choose to change.

questions.stem: In a fair test, what do you call the variable you measure?
questions.explain: Dependent = it depends on what you changed.

questions.stem: What are the variables you keep the same in a fair test called?
questions.explain: Keeping them the same makes the test fair.

questions.stem: In a fair test you change two things at once to save time.
questions.explain: False — change only one thing, or you can't tell which one caused the result.
